meta.name: CCA-P rote-memorization bank
meta.description: Non-inferable knowledge extracted from the five official CCA-P prep course modules: exact terms, values, behaviors, and definitions that must be memorized outright, plus counter-intuitive rules where the course answer contradicts common engineering intuition. Selection criterion: a strong architect who never read the courses could not derive the item by reasoning. Deducible principles are excluded by design.

items.sourceSection: The four properties architects design around
items.lead: A prompt too large to send is rejected before generation

points.v: Exceeds the model's token limit ("prompt too long")
Exceeds the API's byte limit on the raw request body

quiz.q: A batch ingestion service sees two distinct rejection classes when submitting large documents. Neither reaches generation. What separates the two rejections?
options: One is transient rate limiting on the account; the other a permanent quota breach that only a written contract change resolves.
One means the generated output would have been too long; the other means the submitted input itself was far too long.
One means the prompt exceeded the model's token limit; the other that the raw request body exceeded the API's byte limit.
Both originate at an intermediate proxy rather than the API itself, and both signal exactly the same underlying token overflow.
quiz.why: Oversized requests split two ways: invalid_request_error (400) is the model's token limit; request_too_large (413) is the API's byte limit on the raw body.

items.sourceSection: The four properties architects design around
items.lead: When the prompt fits but generation hits the context ceiling

points.v: Stop reason returned; output is truncated — distinct from a rejected oversized request

quiz.q: A summarization service returns responses that stop mid-sentence, yet every call was accepted and returned successfully. Nothing was rejected. What does this indicate?
options: Generation ran into the context ceiling; the response carries a distinct stop reason and truncated output.
The raw request body exceeded the API's documented byte limit and was silently truncated somewhere in transit.
The prompt exceeded the model's token limit, so the request was rejected before generation began.
A gateway timeout cut the stream; retrying the identical prompt always returns the complete answer.
quiz.why: Accepted-then-truncated is the model_context_window_exceeded stop reason. An oversized prompt is rejected before generation, never returned as a successful truncated response.

items.sourceSection: The four properties architects design around
items.lead: Course mitigations mapped to each property

points.v: Citations, uncertainty signaling, generator-verifier loops, routing factual lookups through tools
Web search, retrieval (RAG), tool use, MCP servers as source of truth
Progressive context loading, chunking, front-loading critical information, projects, summarizing across turns
System prompts, structured outputs, code execution

quiz.q: A legal assistant keeps producing confident, well-formed case citations that do not exist. Which mitigation set does the course map to the property responsible?
options: Progressive context loading, chunking, front-loading critical information, and summarizing across turns.
Web search, retrieval, tool use, and MCP servers as the source of truth.
System prompts, structured outputs, and code execution applied to the response.
Citations, uncertainty signaling, generator-verifier loops, and routing factual lookups through tools.
quiz.why: Fabricated-but-fluent output is pattern completion; those are its mitigations. The retrieval list answers knowledge boundaries, chunking answers the context window, system prompts answer steerability.

items.sourceSection: The four properties architects design around
items.lead: The four properties map 1:1 to four design consequences

points.v: Same input, different outputs across runs
Hard edge, fixed token budget
Wrong answers in the same fluent tone as right ones
Reliable on common/recent/consistent topics; unreliable on rare/private/fast-changing ones

quiz.q: An architect briefs a risk committee on the practical consequences the design must absorb, one for each underlying property of the technology. Which set is that?
options: Non-determinism; latency variance across runs; hallucination rate; and the model's fixed training data cutoff date.
Non-determinism; context as a finite resource; confidence is not validity; knowledge and capability boundaries.
Next-token prediction; knowledge; working memory as a hard edge; steerability under instruction.
Cost; latency; reliability under load; observability of the system's real failure modes.
quiz.why: These are the four design consequences; the properties they map from (next-token prediction, knowledge, working memory, steerability) are a different list entirely.

items.sourceSection: Entry points, build-time interfaces, delivery routes
items.lead: Three layers present in every deployment, never alternatives

points.v: What a person/system interacts with: Claude.ai, Claude Code, a custom app
What an engineer programs against: the API, SDKs, MCP, the Agent SDK
Where API traffic terminates: Anthropic, AWS Bedrock, GCP Vertex AI, Microsoft Foundry

quiz.q: In a design review someone asks whether the team should "use Claude Code, or the API, or Bedrock" for the new deployment. How should the architect reframe this?
options: Those are three separate layers — what users touch, what engineers program against, where traffic terminates — present in every deployment.
They are three competing options, and committing to any one of them rules the other two out for the deployment's lifetime.
Only the last two are genuine choices; the first is a consumer product with no architectural role in an enterprise design.
They are the same choice expressed at different abstraction levels; pick whichever one the client already licenses and pays for today.
quiz.why: Entry points, build-time interfaces, and delivery routes are three layers present in every deployment, never alternatives to choose between.

items.sourceSection: Entry points, build-time interfaces, delivery routes

points.v: Claude Code is built for developers running a terminal, not non-engineering end users — even though the same model powers every entry point

items.logic: The entry point, not the underlying model, decides who a product is for.

quiz.q: A bank wants its non-technical operations staff on "the strongest Claude", so an engineer proposes rolling out the terminal-based coding product to them. What is the flaw?
options: The underlying model differs per entry point, so that product would actually hand them a materially weaker model.
Nothing — the same model powers every entry point, so which product they use does not affect who it suits.
The same model powers every entry point; that product is built for developers in a terminal, not non-engineering users.
The flaw is purely licensing: that product cannot be procured for non-engineering headcount under the organisation's current enterprise agreement.
quiz.why: Claude Code targets developers running a terminal. Identical model quality across entry points does not make it fit non-engineering users; the entry point decides audience.

items.sourceSection: The parts an architect assembles solutions from

points.v: A function the model can call to act or fetch
Protocol exposing tools so multiple Claude clients reach the same entry points
Scoped sub-task in a separate context, isolated or parallel
Deterministic code firing on defined events to enforce a rule the model cannot skip
Versioned reusable unit — instructions plus optional scripts
Coordinated peer agents each owning part of a goal
Steps assembled at runtime rather than fixed in advance

quiz.q: A regulated client needs a redaction step that runs on every file write and that the model has no way to bypass or forget. Which primitive does that?
options: A skill — a versioned, reusable unit of instructions plus optional scripts that the model loads when relevant.
A subagent — a scoped sub-task running in its own separate context, isolated from the main run.
A tool — a function the model can call to act on or fetch something it needs.
A hook — deterministic code firing on a defined event to enforce a rule the model cannot skip.
quiz.why: Hooks are deterministic code on defined events, unskippable by the model. A tool runs only if the model chooses to call it; skills and subagents are likewise model-mediated.

items.sourceSection: The parts an architect assembles solutions from

points.v: Steps wired in your code, often using tools
The model choosing its own sequence of tool calls
An orchestrator delegating to subagents

quiz.q: Two engineers disagree: one says the model is driving their system because it calls tools; the other says it is not, because the call order is fixed in their own code. Who is right?
options: The first: any system that calls tools at all qualifies under the reserved term, regardless of who fixed the ordering.
The second: steps wired in your code, even using tools, is a workflow; an agent picks its own sequence.
Neither: a system that calls tools in any fixed order is by definition a multi-agent system under the reserved terms.
The first: a fixed ordering still qualifies whenever a model decides each individual tool call's arguments at runtime.
quiz.why: Reserved definitions: workflow = steps wired in your code, agent = the model choosing its own tool-call sequence, multi-agent = an orchestrator delegating to subagents.

items.topic: Delegation map and its three tests
items.sourceSection: Where Claude fits (Claude / systems / humans)
items.lead: Decomposition produces a delegation map assigning each request part

points.v: Category Claude should handle
Category a human must handle
Claude drafts, a person decides
Reversibility, Stakes, Accountability — justify each assignment

quiz.q: An architect splits a claims process into parts Claude handles, parts people keep, and parts where Claude drafts and a person decides. A reviewer asks what justifies each assignment.
options: Cost, latency, and observability, measured for each step in the overall process.
Accuracy scores measured on the curated eval set covering each step of the process.
Reversibility, stakes, and accountability — three tests applied to justify each individual assignment.
Predictability, error cost, and the recurring run cost attached to each assignment.
quiz.why: The delegation map's three tests are reversibility, stakes, and accountability. The other lists are pattern-selection factors, not the justification for how work is delegated.

items.sourceSection: Three patterns for structuring Claude's involvement
items.lead: In production, agents are bound by four non-optional things

points.v: Constrained tool entry points
Per-turn budgets
Explicit permissions
Stopping criteria

quiz.q: A team is promoting an autonomous system from prototype to production and asks what becomes non-optional at that boundary. Which four things?
options: Constrained tool entry points, per-turn budgets, explicit permissions, and stopping criteria on every run.
Fine-tuned weights, pinned prompts, cached prefixes, and shadow traffic mirrored on every call.
Rate limits, retries with exponential backoff, circuit breakers, and tiered fallback chains.
A router, an evaluator, an optimizer, and a coverage check performed at synthesis.
quiz.why: In production, agents are bound by constrained tool entry points, per-turn budgets, explicit permissions, and stopping criteria — the four non-optional bindings.

items.sourceSection: Try prompting before you consider fine-tuning
items.lead: Anthropic's recommended reliability sequence, in order

points.v: Optimize the prompt
Add tool use or retrieval
Move to a stronger pattern such as evaluator-optimizer
Only then consider fine-tuning

quiz.q: Accuracy on a classification feature is short of target, and the client proposes training a custom model immediately. What does Anthropic's recommended order say to do first?
options: Add tool use first, then move to a stronger pattern, then optimize the prompt if still short.
Optimize the prompt, then add tool use or retrieval, then move to a stronger pattern such as evaluator-optimizer.
Run an eval, then swap to the most capable tier, then customise the model's weights on their data.
Move straight to an evaluator-optimizer pattern; prompt work rarely moves accuracy by any meaningful margin.
quiz.why: The recommended sequence is prompt optimization, then tool use or retrieval, then a stronger pattern such as evaluator-optimizer, and only then fine-tuning.

items.sourceSection: Try prompting before you consider fine-tuning

points.v: Fine-tuning access is limited, varies by model and delivery route, and changes as the program expands — confirm current options with the Anthropic account team before recommending it

quiz.q: A client asks the architect to commit in the statement of work to customising model weights on their chosen cloud route. What is the correct response?
options: Commit it; weight customisation is generally available across all four delivery routes today, on every current model.
Refuse outright; weight customisation is never available on any Anthropic model at all, through any delivery route, under any contract whatsoever.
Commit it for the direct API only, since cloud-mediated routes never support weight customisation at all today.
Confirm current options with the Anthropic account team first — access is limited and varies by model and delivery route.
quiz.why: Fine-tuning access is limited, varies by model and delivery route, and changes as the program expands — confirm with the Anthropic account team before recommending it.

items.sourceSection: Skills-based architecture as a packaging option

points.v: Cost is driven by accumulated context and number of model calls, not by pattern label; a poorly designed workflow can cost more than a well-designed agent

items.logic: Agents are assumed to automatically cost more than workflows because of the label alone.

quiz.q: A finance stakeholder rejects a proposed design on cost grounds, pointing at the word "agent" in the diagram and demanding the alternative structure. What should the architect say?
options: The label does not set cost; accumulated context and number of model calls do — a poor workflow can cost more.
Agents inherently cost more than workflows, so the stakeholder is right to demand the alternative structure on budget grounds.
Cost is set by the model tier alone, so the structural pattern chosen is irrelevant to the budget.
Agents cost strictly less by definition, because they stop as soon as the stated goal has been met.
quiz.why: Cost is driven by accumulated context and the number of model calls, not the pattern label; a poorly designed workflow can outspend a well-designed agent.

items.sourceSection: When the team wanted flexibility and got non-determinism

points.v: Trace mining usually shows real task paths fall into a handful of enumerable shapes — a router plus a few chains was correct all along

items.logic: Feeling uncertain how to structure a task is mistaken for proof the task needs an agent's flexibility.

quiz.q: A team could not agree how to structure a support-triage task, so they built the most flexible thing available. Six months of traces now exist. What do such traces typically show?
options: The task's genuine open-endedness is confirmed by the traces, justifying the flexible design after all the debate.
Paths are distributed almost perfectly uniformly, so no useful routing rule can be derived from any of the trace data at all.
Real task paths fall into a handful of enumerable shapes; a router plus a few chains was correct all along.
Mostly tool errors, so the correct fix is better tool descriptions rather than restructuring anything at this stage.
quiz.why: Uncertainty about how to structure a task is not evidence the task is open-ended; trace mining usually enumerates a handful of shapes a router can cover.

items.sourceSection: What broke and why

points.v: An auditor can point to a discrete code step
An auditor can only point to a model turn — the compliance risk the agent pattern itself introduces
A governance gap under any pattern, not agent-specific

items.logic: The two failures get lumped together as one agent problem; only the missing discrete approval step is agent-pattern-specific.

quiz.q: A post-incident review lists two findings: an approval that exists only as a model turn no auditor can point to, and a model version that was never pinned. Which is pattern-specific?
options: Both — each one stems directly from letting the model drive its own sequence.
Only the unauditable approval; an unpinned version is a governance gap under any pattern.
Only the unpinned version; approval steps are never auditable under any pattern at all.
Neither; both are ordinary operational hygiene, entirely unrelated to the chosen pattern.
quiz.why: The agent pattern itself introduces the risk that an auditor can point only to a model turn. An unpinned model version is a pattern-independent governance gap.

items.sourceSection: What broke: a deterministic rule handed to a probabilistic system

points.v: Logging that catches a broken deterministic check (e.g. a SQL rule) doesn't record choices a model makes inside a request; a business rule folded into a probabilistic system drifts silently, surfacing only via manual audit

items.logic: Existing production monitoring is assumed to flag a broken business rule the way it flags a broken query.

quiz.q: A discount-eligibility rule was moved out of SQL and into the prompt. The team keeps its existing monitoring, reasoning that it already alerts when that rule breaks. What actually happens?
options: Alerting keeps working exactly as it did before, since the rule's outputs still land in the very same database tables downstream as always.
The rule fails loudly and often, producing far more alerts than the SQL version ever did in production.
Latency monitoring catches it indirectly, because drifted decisions consistently take measurably longer to produce than correct ones.
The rule drifts silently — existing logging does not record choices the model makes inside a request; only manual audit surfaces it.
quiz.why: Monitoring that flags a broken deterministic check does not capture model decisions inside a request. A business rule folded into a probabilistic system drifts silently.

items.sourceSection: Error recovery: where a failure can be caught, and where it cannot

points.v: Usually recoverable — retry, reroute, or drop and flag the gap
Usually not recoverable — the whole run fails and partial subagent work is stranded

items.logic: Recoverability is assumed symmetric, or the orchestrator assumed more robust for being "in charge"; it is actually the single point of failure.

quiz.q: A fan-out research system is being hardened. The team asks where to concentrate its retry and resilience budget, since failures can occur at either level.
options: Spend it on the coordinator: worker failures are usually recoverable by retry or reroute, coordinator failure strands the run.
Spread it evenly across both levels, since they fail and recover in broadly comparable ways in practice.
Spend it on the workers, the single point of failure; the coordinator is inherently more robust for being in charge.
Neither; recovery belongs entirely to the caller, which simply retries the whole job from the very beginning.
quiz.why: Recoverability is asymmetric. Subagent failure is usually recoverable — retry, reroute, or drop and flag. Orchestrator failure fails the run and strands partial work.

items.sourceSection: Human-in-the-loop checkpoint patterns for agent workflows
items.lead: A checkpoint gates execution for review, positioned by risk and reversibility

points.v: Every irreversible or high-stakes action
Lower-stakes actions rather than gating each one

quiz.q: An agent performs thousands of low-stakes tag updates plus a handful of irreversible account closures. A reviewer wants human review without destroying throughput. What positioning?
options: Gate everything; sampling leaves an unreviewed path and is never acceptable in a production system.
Gate every irreversible or high-stakes action; sample the lower-stakes ones rather than gating each.
Sample both categories at an identical rate, which keeps the review workload predictable week to week.
Gate the high-volume actions, since that is where most of the total risk accumulates.
quiz.why: Checkpoints are positioned by risk and reversibility: gate every irreversible or high-stakes action, and sample lower-stakes ones. Volume is not the criterion.

items.sourceSection: When fan-out hid a dropped unit
items.lead: The most dangerous multi-agent failure is silent

points.v: A subagent drops a unit and the orchestrator synthesizes a confident, complete-looking answer
Coverage check at synthesis — results returned must equal units dispatched, or flag the difference

quiz.q: A fan-out summarizer dispatched forty documents. The final report reads as complete and confident, but one document was never summarized and no error was raised. What is the fix?
options: Raise the orchestrator's model tier so it reliably notices the missing material on its own.
Retry every subagent call twice, which statistically eliminates dropped units at an acceptable cost.
Add a coverage check at synthesis: results returned must equal units dispatched, or flag the difference.
Increase the context window so that all forty documents fit comfortably into a single call.
quiz.why: The dangerous multi-agent failure is silent: a dropped unit plus a confident, complete-looking synthesis. The fix is a coverage check reconciling results returned against units dispatched.

items.sourceSection: Reference architectures: what good looks like and where projects go wrong
items.lead: The good-vs-broken pattern for structured extraction

points.v: OCR, extract fields against a schema, validate, route exceptions
Common because first-pass extraction on edge cases isn't trustworthy unchecked
No exception path — low-confidence extractions flow through same pipeline as clean documents, no human gate

quiz.q: An invoice extraction service processes clean scans and smudged faxes identically, end to end, and no human ever sees the doubtful ones. What is missing?
options: OCR preprocessing, without which the smudged faxes cannot reliably be read by the extractor at all.
A schema — those fields ought to be extracted free-form first and then normalised downstream in a later separate step.
A larger context window, so that whole invoice batches fit comfortably into one single request.
An exception path — low-confidence extractions flow through the same pipeline as clean documents with no human gate.
quiz.why: The structured-extraction failure mode is no exception path. The pipeline is OCR, schema-bound extraction, validation, and routing exceptions, with evaluator-optimizer checking untrustworthy first passes.

items.sourceSection: How to decide if a problem needs one or several patterns

points.v: Composing two reference architectures requires separate eval sets per architecture, not one for the composed system

items.logic: A single end-to-end score can hide a broken component behind a healthy aggregate.

quiz.q: A design combines document extraction with a retrieval-backed question-answering surface. The team plans to measure quality with one score on the finished system. What should the architect require?
options: Separate eval sets, one per architecture, rather than a single set for the composed system.
One end-to-end score is right, since that is exactly what the users actually experience.
A single eval set, plus human review of any run scoring below the agreed threshold.
No evals until the composition stabilises, since measuring a moving target simply wastes reviewer effort.
quiz.why: Composing two reference architectures requires separate eval sets per architecture. A single end-to-end score can hide a broken component behind a healthy aggregate.

items.sourceSection: The retrieval principle

points.v: For stable knowledge — true yesterday and tomorrow
For live state — a current value owned by a system, changing independently of your index
The most common reference-architecture mistake — produces fluent, confident, wrong answers with no error signal

quiz.q: A support assistant must answer both "what does our refund policy say" and "what is the balance on this account right now". How should each be sourced?
options: Both from the vector index, refreshed frequently enough that it stays acceptably current at all times.
Both by tool call, since retrieval adds latency without improving accuracy on either kind of question.
The policy from retrieval over stable knowledge; the balance by calling the system that owns it.
The policy by tool call to the CMS; the balance from the index, cheaper at scale.
quiz.why: Retrieval is for stable knowledge; tool use is for live state owned by another system. Conflating the two is the most common reference-architecture mistake.

items.sourceSection: Chunking: how you break the corpus, by what the corpus is

points.v: The chunking approach is chosen by the structure of the source material, never by a default or fixed chunk size

items.logic: Teams default to a universal fixed chunk size (e.g. 500 tokens) instead of deriving it from the document.

quiz.q: A team is onboarding three corpora — numbered regulations, narrative incident write-ups, and call transcripts — and asks what to set as the standard split size across all of them.
options: 500 tokens with overlap, the well-established default that works across most enterprise corpora.
There is no standard size: the approach follows the structure of each source material.
Whatever size keeps embedding cost within budget, since structure barely affects retrieval recall.
The model's context window divided by the top-k retrieval count you intend to use.
quiz.why: The chunking approach is chosen by the structure of the source material, never by a default or a fixed chunk size applied uniformly across corpora.

items.sourceSection: Articulating the trade-off
items.lead: Every retrieval design trades retrieval quality, latency, and maintenance

points.v: Raises quality and latency together
Lowers latency and maintenance but misses exact-match queries

quiz.q: A team is choosing between two index configurations and wants to know what each one buys and what it costs, given a tight SLA and a small maintenance budget.
options: Smaller chunks with hybrid indexing lower latency and raise quality at the same time; there is no real trade-off to model.
Larger chunks with dense-only indexing raise both quality and latency; smaller chunks cut both of them at once.
Chunk size affects only storage cost, while the indexing strategy alone determines retrieval quality and end-to-end latency.
Smaller chunks with hybrid indexing raise quality and latency together; larger chunks with dense-only lower latency but miss exact-match queries.
quiz.why: Every retrieval design trades retrieval quality, latency, and maintenance. Smaller chunks plus hybrid indexing buy quality at a latency cost; the dense-only option misses exact-match queries.

items.sourceSection: Design the RAG pipeline

points.v: Hierarchical chunking preserving section/subsection structure so a clause or procedure stays intact
Semantic chunking on meaning boundaries so each passage is self-contained
Cut mid-idea and across section boundaries — the failure mode

quiz.q: One corpus is a numbered policy manual with clauses and subsections; another is long-form prose with no headings or anchors at all. How should each be split?
options: Both by fixed size, tuned per corpus to the average passage length observed there.
The manual hierarchically, preserving section structure; the prose semantically, on natural meaning boundaries.
The manual semantically, since numbering is arbitrary; the prose hierarchically by paragraph count.
The manual by fixed size, since its clauses are short; the prose hierarchically instead.
quiz.why: Structured, section-numbered sources take hierarchical chunking so a clause stays intact; anchorless prose takes semantic chunking. Fixed-size chunks cut mid-idea and across section boundaries.

items.sourceSection: Distinct terms that are easy to conflate

points.v: The model has no native memory between calls; persistence exists only because the application stored and passed it back in — an architectural choice, not a model capability

quiz.q: A product manager asks whether the assistant "remembers" a customer between sessions, and whether that is simply a setting somebody has to enable. What is the accurate answer?
options: The model has no memory between calls; persistence exists only because the application stored it and passed it back.
There is a retention setting; enabling it makes the model recall prior sessions for that customer.
The model recalls prior calls made under the same API key for a rolling retention window.
Memory is inherent to the model but capped at the context window's size across all sessions.
quiz.why: There is no native memory between calls. Persistence is an architectural choice — the application stores context and passes it back in — not a model capability.

items.sourceSection: Model selection: start with Sonnet, move deliberately
items.lead: Sonnet is the default; move only on eval evidence

points.v: Most capable — demanding reasoning, advanced coding, research synthesis
Default starting point
Only when an eval set shows Sonnet misses the quality bar
Only when an eval set confirms the tradeoff is acceptable

quiz.q: A team is starting a new deployment and debating which tier to build on, with one engineer arguing for the most capable option from day one. What is the guidance?
options: Start on the most capable tier that is available, then step down later, once quality on real production traffic has been proven adequate.
Start on the cheapest available tier and move up whenever users begin complaining about answer quality in the support queue.
Pick by input length alone: the tier simply follows the largest document you must process in production.
Start on Sonnet; move up only when an eval shows it misses the bar, down only when an eval confirms the tradeoff.
quiz.why: Sonnet is the default starting point. Moving to Opus requires eval evidence that Sonnet misses the bar; moving to Haiku requires eval evidence the tradeoff is acceptable.

items.topic: Token counts are measured, not estimated
items.sourceSection: Context-window sizing: the working-memory cliff
items.lead: Token limits and billing run on measured counts, not estimates

points.v: Every API response reports actual token counts in the usage field
These measured counts — not a characters-per-token estimate, which varies by model generation, tokenizer, and language — govern the context limit and billing
Use to check before sending

quiz.q: A team sizes prompts with a characters-per-token rule of thumb and is surprised that bills and limit errors do not match its spreadsheet. What should it use instead?
options: A more accurate divisor, recalibrated per language from a large sample of real production traffic.
The advertised context window divided by the average number of requests seen per session.
The actual counts reported in each response's usage field, plus the token-counting API before sending.
Byte length of the request body, which is what the API uses to enforce the limit.
quiz.why: Measured token counts — reported in the usage field, checkable via the token-counting API — govern the context limit and billing. Estimates vary by tokenizer, model generation, and language.

items.sourceSection: Context-window sizing: the working-memory cliff

points.v: Budget largest realistic conversation + retrieved context + system prompt + working scratch + growth margin — never the full window

items.logic: Using as much of the advertised window as possible looks efficient, but designing toward the ceiling guarantees overflow in production.

quiz.q: An architect sizes a chat deployment so a typical session plus its retrieved passages fills the model's advertised capacity almost exactly, calling anything less wasteful. What is wrong?
options: The budget must cover the largest realistic conversation plus retrieved context, system prompt, working scratch, and a growth margin.
Nothing at all — leaving expensive paid headroom permanently unused is genuinely wasteful once the deployment reaches real scale.
The error is using the advertised number at all; effective usable capacity is always exactly half of it.
The problem is purely cost, not correctness, because any overflow simply truncates the oldest turns away harmlessly.
quiz.why: The context window is a ceiling, not a target. Budget the largest realistic conversation plus retrieval, system prompt, scratch, and growth margin; designing to the ceiling guarantees overflow.

items.sourceSection: Context strategy: spectrum between progressive and monolithic

points.v: Bounded tasks with predictable input size, stable prefixes for prompt caching, single-shot Q&A, reasoning needing simultaneous access to all material
As context accumulates turn over turn — cost and latency scale linearly with input length; attention quality can degrade before the hard limit

quiz.q: A team loads everything up front in a single call, and it works beautifully on single-shot questions with predictable inputs. Where will this approach stop working?
options: Immediately, unless prompt caching is first disabled, since stable cacheable prefixes conflict directly with loading everything up front.
As context accumulates turn over turn — cost and latency scale linearly with input length and attention can degrade before the limit.
Only at the hard token limit; below that boundary, both cost and answer quality stay essentially flat throughout the session.
On bounded tasks with predictable input size, which is precisely where staging context just-in-time becomes mandatory instead.
quiz.why: A monolithic context earns its place on bounded, predictable tasks with stable cacheable prefixes. It breaks down as context accumulates: linear cost and latency, degrading attention before the limit.

items.sourceSection: Context strategy: spectrum between progressive and monolithic

points.v: Stages context just-in-time — retrieve, summarize across turns, load only what the next step needs
"The right default for most production workloads"
Long-range coherence, decisions depending on detail dropped earlier, and prompt caching; the exact input seen at step N is no longer reconstructable

quiz.q: A long research session stages only what each step needs, retrieving and summarizing as it goes. Reviewers ask what this approach costs them and whether they should standardise on it.
options: It is a niche choice; loading everything up front remains the right default for the great majority of production workloads today.
It is the right default and carries no significant downside at all once retrieval quality is good enough.
It is the right default for most production workloads, but costs long-range coherence, decisions needing dropped detail, and prompt caching.
It is the right default, and it improves prompt caching too, because each step's prefix is much smaller.
quiz.why: Progressive context staging is the right default for most production workloads. It breaks down on long-range coherence, decisions needing earlier detail, and caching — step N's input is unreconstructable.

items.sourceSection: Context strategy: spectrum between progressive and monolithic

points.v: Long-running agents, phase transitions that can checkpoint to a clean summary, sessions that would otherwise hit context limits mid-task

Summaries drop load-bearing detail (identifiers, numeric values, prior decisions, edge cases); the summarizer is itself a model call, compaction is largely one-way, and summary fidelity is an unsolved eval problem

quiz.q: A long-running agent checkpoints to a clean summary at each phase transition so the session never hits its limits mid-task. What is the principal risk being accepted?
options: The extra latency of one more model call; summary fidelity itself is by now a solved measurement problem.
The agent can no longer call any tools at all once the first checkpoint has been written.
Cost roughly doubles, since both the new summary and the original transcript are resent on every subsequent turn.
Summaries drop load-bearing detail — identifiers, numbers, prior decisions, edge cases — and the process is largely one-way.
quiz.why: Compaction earns its place at phase transitions, but summaries drop load-bearing detail (identifiers, numbers, prior decisions), the summarizer is itself a model call, and fidelity is unsolved.

items.sourceSection: In practice, strategies may be combined

points.v: Context strategy (progressive vs monolithic, etc.) and context sizing are separate decisions that interact but don't determine each other

items.logic: Picking a strategy is assumed to settle how much context to budget; treating them as one is where most context designs go wrong.

quiz.q: A design doc records "progressive" under context and leaves the budget section blank, on the grounds that the first entry already answers the second. What is the error?
options: None — staging context just-in-time genuinely does make an explicit budget unnecessary in this design.
They are separate decisions that interact but do not determine each other; both must be made explicitly.
The error is choosing that approach at all before the context budget number is even known.
The budget section is only ever needed for monolithic designs, so the doc is fine as written.
quiz.why: Context strategy and context sizing are separate decisions. Treating one as settling the other is where most context designs go wrong.

items.topic: Adaptive thinking and the effort parameter
items.sourceSection: What extended thinking controls

points.v: On Claude Opus 4.6 and later, Claude Sonnet 4.6 and later, and Claude Sonnet 5, adaptive thinking with the effort parameter is the recommended control — set reasoning effort, not a token budget

quiz.q: A team on the current Sonnet generation wants finer control over how much reasoning each request performs. What is the recommended control?
options: Set the reasoning effort via the effort parameter, using adaptive thinking.
Set an explicit token budget for reasoning on every outgoing request.
Switch model tiers per request; reasoning depth is not otherwise adjustable.
Raise max_tokens, which proportionally increases the depth of the reasoning performed.
quiz.why: On Opus 4.6 and later, Sonnet 4.6 and later, and Sonnet 5, adaptive thinking with the effort parameter is recommended — set reasoning effort, not a token budget.

items.sourceSection: What extended thinking controls

points.v: Adaptive thinking is the only thinking mode on Claude Fable 5

quiz.q: An integration is being ported to Claude Fable 5, and the team asks which reasoning modes they can choose between on that model.
options: Two: a fixed-budget mode and an adaptive mode, selected per individual request.
Three, matching the three effort levels available on the other current models.
One: adaptive thinking is the only thinking mode available on that model.
None at all; reasoning control is entirely unavailable on that particular model.
quiz.why: Adaptive thinking is the only thinking mode on Claude Fable 5; there is no alternative mode to select.

items.sourceSection: What extended thinking controls

points.v: Deprecated on the 4.6 model generation; removed on Claude Sonnet 5, where passing it returns a 400 error

quiz.q: A service that ran unchanged for a year starts failing with 400 errors immediately after a model upgrade. Nobody touched the request body. What is the likely cause?
options: The prompt now exceeds the newer model's smaller advertised token limit and is therefore rejected.
The API version header must always be bumped alongside any change of the model identifier.
The new model requires the effort parameter to be set explicitly, or it rejects the call.
A parameter deprecated on the previous generation and removed on the new model is still in the request.
quiz.why: budget_tokens was deprecated on the 4.6 model generation and removed on Claude Sonnet 5, where passing it returns a 400 error.

items.sourceSection: What extended thinking controls

points.v: Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens at the model's standard output rate and add latency; when extended thinking is not engaged, none are generated or billed

quiz.q: Finance asks how the extra reasoning pass shows up on the invoice, and what it costs on requests where it is not engaged at all.
options: Billed as output tokens at the standard output rate, and nothing is generated or billed when it is not engaged.
Billed as input tokens at a heavily discounted rate, with a small standing charge applied even when it goes entirely unused.
Billed at a dedicated reasoning rate, plus a flat per-request surcharge applied on top of the usual cost.
Not billed at all; only the visible response text is ever charged for anywhere on the invoice.
quiz.why: Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens at the model's standard output rate and add latency. When extended thinking is not engaged, none are generated or billed.

items.sourceSection: What extended thinking controls

points.v: The model reasons internally either way; the toggle controls only whether you spend tokens and latency on an additional billed, expanded reasoning pass

items.logic: Disabling extended thinking is assumed to make the model skip reasoning entirely.

quiz.q: To cut cost a team turns the extra reasoning pass off, and warns stakeholders that answers will now be produced "without any reasoning at all". Is that right?
options: Yes — with it switched off the model emits tokens directly, with no internal reasoning step whatsoever.
No — the model reasons internally either way; the toggle only controls paying tokens and latency for an extra expanded pass.
No — the toggle only changes whether the reasoning is shown, and the billing is identical either way.
Yes, and the output quality is therefore always materially worse on every request where it is turned off.
quiz.why: The extended-thinking toggle does not switch reasoning on or off. The model reasons internally regardless; the toggle decides whether you spend tokens and latency on an extra billed pass.

items.sourceSection: What extended thinking controls

points.v: The API may return a summarized representation of the thinking process, but billing is for thinking tokens actually consumed during reasoning, not the length of the visible summary

items.logic: A short visible summary suggests small billing, while actual internal consumption can be far larger.

quiz.q: An engineer reconciles the bill against the reasoning text visible in API responses and finds far more charged than that visible text could account for. Explanation?
options: A billing defect: charged reasoning ought to match the returned reasoning text exactly, token for token.
Silent retries doubled the reasoning charge on every affected request, without ever appearing in the logs.
Visible text is charged at output rates and the remainder at input rates, inflating the total.
The API may return only a summarized representation; billing reflects thinking tokens actually consumed during reasoning.
quiz.why: Extended thinking may be returned as a summary. Billing is for thinking tokens actually consumed, not the length of the visible summary, so short summaries can carry large charges.

items.sourceSection: Gate every model change with an eval before you ship it
items.lead: Treat any model change like a code deployment

points.v: Curated prompts with known-good outputs covering the real production distribution
Model-graded against a rubric, or programmatic
Set in advance — below it, you do not ship

quiz.q: A newer model is available and the team wants to switch next sprint. What three artifacts does the architect require before that swap is allowed to ship?
options: A full load test, a cost projection for the new model, and a thoroughly documented rollback runbook for operations.
A shadow deployment, a small canary cohort, and a post-hoc quality review conducted after launch.
A curated test set with known-good outputs, a grading function, and a delta/rollback threshold set in advance.
A public benchmark comparison, a latency budget for the change, and written account-team sign-off.
quiz.why: Treat a model change like a code deployment: a test set covering the real production distribution, a grading function (model-graded or programmatic), and a pre-set rollback threshold.

items.sourceSection: Gate every model change with an eval before you ship it

points.v: The rollback threshold must be set before running the eval, not after

items.logic: Deciding an acceptable gap after seeing results rationalizes the threshold to match the outcome.

quiz.q: An eval run comes back showing a 4% quality gap on the candidate model, and the team convenes to decide whether 4% is acceptable. What went wrong procedurally?
options: The threshold had to be set before running the eval; deciding afterwards rationalizes it to fit the result.
Nothing; judging the observed gap in context is exactly how such a decision should be made.
The gap should have been measured against a public benchmark rather than an internal test set.
Nothing procedural at all, though a 4% delta is always below any threshold worth shipping against.
quiz.why: The delta/rollback threshold must be set in advance. Deciding an acceptable gap after seeing results rationalizes the threshold to match the outcome.

items.topic: No tier decision = most expensive tier
items.sourceSection: How a model-tier decision becomes a budget conversation

points.v: Not choosing a model tier is choosing the most expensive one; a system with no per-step model-tier decision defaults to the priciest option

quiz.q: A multi-step pipeline shipped without anyone specifying which model each step should call. Finance asks what that implies for spend.
options: Spend is unpredictable, but it averages out to roughly the mid-tier price across all of the steps.
The system defaults to the priciest option — not choosing a tier is choosing the most expensive one.
Nothing yet; cost follows total token volume, not which particular model happens to run each individual step.
The platform automatically routes each step to the cheapest model that is sufficient for that particular step.
quiz.why: A system with no per-step model-tier decision defaults to the most expensive tier. Not choosing is choosing the priciest option.

items.sourceSection: Decision: identify the load-bearing control
items.lead: The load-bearing control is the setting that breaches budget first if relaxed

points.v: Model tier and extended thinking are load-bearing
Model tier and context strategy are load-bearing

quiz.q: A deployment misses its p95 response-time target. Which settings would breach that target first if relaxed, and are therefore the ones to tune?
options: Chunk size and index type in the retrieval layer.
Retry policy and circuit-breaker thresholds at the service boundary.
Model tier and the context strategy that was chosen.
Model tier and whether extended thinking is enabled.
quiz.why: The load-bearing control breaches budget first if relaxed. Latency binding makes model tier and extended thinking load-bearing; cost binding makes model tier and context strategy.

items.sourceSection: Description: the 4D competency applied to prompt design
items.lead: Description (an AI Fluency competency) names what you want precisely

points.v: What is in and out of bounds
The exact output contract
Rules that must never be violated

quiz.q: A prompt keeps producing outputs the team fixes by hand, and the diagnosis is that the request itself was never stated precisely enough. Which three things must it name?
options: Persona, tone of voice, and worked examples.
Inputs, outputs, and error handling.
Scope, output format, and hard constraints.
Role, task, and evaluation rubric.
quiz.why: Description, an AI Fluency competency, names what you want precisely: scope (in and out of bounds), format (the exact output contract), and constraints (rules never to violate).

items.sourceSection: Skills as an integration mechanism

points.v: Parameter that attaches a Skill to a request
Endpoint for publishing and versioning Skills
Skills require the Code Execution Tool, so the pattern always carries a sandboxed execution environment dependency

quiz.q: A partner wants to attach a versioned, reusable unit of instructions plus scripts to its API requests. The security team asks what infrastructure dependency that introduces.
options: A vector index, since the unit's contents must be retrieved at call time.
A sandboxed execution environment, because the pattern requires the Code Execution Tool.
A dedicated MCP server, which is how such units are published and discovered.
None; the unit is simply inlined into the system prompt at request time.
quiz.why: Skills attach via the container.skills parameter and are published and versioned at /v1/skills, and they require the Code Execution Tool — always a sandboxed execution dependency.

items.sourceSection: A way to keep these terms separate
items.lead: The SDK is an opinionated wrapper over the same API entry point

points.v: Python, TypeScript, Java, Go, Ruby, C#, PHP
Only for a freshly shipped API feature not yet in the SDK

quiz.q: A polyglot enterprise asks which of its stacks can use the official wrapper library, and when its teams would ever hand-roll HTTP calls instead.
options: Python, TypeScript, Java, Go, Ruby, C#, and PHP; drop to raw HTTP only for a freshly shipped feature.
Python and TypeScript only; every other stack in the estate has to call raw HTTP directly instead.
Any language at all via generated clients; raw HTTP is required whenever tool use is involved.
Python, TypeScript, Java, and Go only; raw HTTP is preferred for any genuinely high-throughput service.
quiz.why: SDKs cover Python, TypeScript, Java, Go, Ruby, C#, and PHP — opinionated wrappers over the same API. Drop to raw HTTP only for a feature not yet in the SDK.

items.sourceSection: A way to keep these terms separate

points.v: The protocol for exposing and discovering a tool entry point across clients
How Claude calls a tool inside a single request (an MCP server's tools are invoked via API tool use)
When one tool entry point must be reachable from multiple Claude clients
When the tools live inside one product

quiz.q: A company's ticketing integration must be usable from the desktop app, the terminal tool, and a custom internal product. What should the team build?
options: Three separate per-product tool definitions, since tool schemas cannot be shared across different clients.
Raw API tool use inside each product, which is recommended whenever several clients are involved.
An MCP server, so one tool entry point is reachable from multiple Claude clients.
A shared prompt library; tool definitions themselves are not reusable across separate clients.
quiz.why: MCP is the protocol for exposing and discovering a tool entry point across clients. Raw API tool use fits when the tools live inside a single product.

items.sourceSection: Claude Agent SDK: when a partner needs an agent loop they can embed in their own product

points.v: Wraps API boilerplate but does not run an agent loop
Managed runtime that runs the agent loop powering Claude Code, distributed as @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk for TypeScript and Python

quiz.q: A partner wants to embed the same agent loop that powers the terminal coding product inside their own application. Which package, and what does the ordinary one not do?
options: The ordinary SDK already runs a complete agent loop on its own, so no additional package is needed at all.
The MCP server package, which supplies both the agent loop and the tool definitions together.
A raw HTTP client; the loop has to be hand-written, since no package exposes it directly.
@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk — a managed runtime running the agent loop; the ordinary SDK wraps API boilerplate but runs no loop.
quiz.why: The Anthropic SDK wraps API boilerplate without running an agent loop. The Claude Agent SDK is the managed runtime powering Claude Code, shipped for TypeScript and Python.

items.sourceSection: Claude Code: customization and governance layers

points.k: What the agent knows and does
points.v: CLAUDE.md, skills, subagents, MCP

points.k: What the agent is allowed to touch
points.v: Hooks, permission boundaries, approval flows, sandboxing, restricted execution

quiz.q: A platform team writing governance policy for the terminal coding tool wants to separate configuration that shapes behaviour from configuration that limits blast radius. Which split?
options: CLAUDE.md and hooks shape what it knows and does; skills, subagents, and MCP bound what the agent is allowed to touch.
CLAUDE.md, skills, subagents, and MCP shape what it knows and does; hooks, permissions, approvals, sandboxing, and restricted execution bound what it touches.
MCP and sandboxing shape what it knows and does; CLAUDE.md and permission boundaries bound what the agent touches in the repository.
All of these shape behaviour equally; blast radius is instead controlled entirely at the network and filesystem layer.
quiz.why: The two layer groups are what the agent knows and does (CLAUDE.md, skills, subagents, MCP) and what it is allowed to touch (hooks, permissions, approvals, sandboxing, restricted execution).

items.sourceSection: CSP delivery routes: where API traffic terminates
items.lead: The same model is available through four delivery routes

points.v: Direct Anthropic API (api.anthropic.com)
AWS Bedrock
GCP Vertex AI
Microsoft Foundry (Azure)
Which cloud account the spend lands in, which identity system authenticates, which region traffic terminates in, which procurement contract covers it — not behavior

quiz.q: A bank's procurement team asks what actually changes if they consume Claude through their existing AWS contract instead of directly. What is the honest answer?
options: Which cloud account the spend lands in, which identity system authenticates, which region traffic terminates in, and which contract covers it.
Model behavior differs measurably between the four routes, so every eval has to be re-run separately per route before any production launch.
Nothing whatsoever; the four routes are fully interchangeable in every single respect that could matter to procurement.
Only the price; identity, region, and contracting are all handled identically across every one of the four routes.
quiz.why: The same model is available through the Anthropic API, AWS Bedrock, GCP Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry. What differs is spend, identity, region, and procurement — not behavior.

items.sourceSection: CSP delivery routes: where API traffic terminates

points.v: CSP-mediated routes (Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry) tend to lag the first-party API on new features by weeks, sometimes longer for major capabilities

quiz.q: A client on a cloud marketplace route asks when a just-announced capability will be usable in their environment. What expectation should the architect set?
options: Simultaneously; capability announcements are always coordinated across every delivery route well in advance.
Only at their cloud provider's next quarterly release train, always exactly one quarter behind.
Never; cloud routes only ever receive stable capabilities from the previous model generation.
Typically weeks behind the first-party API, and sometimes considerably longer for major capabilities.
quiz.why: CSP-mediated routes — Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry — tend to lag the first-party API by weeks, sometimes longer for major capabilities.

items.sourceSection: CSP delivery routes: where API traffic terminates
items.lead: Across routes the wrapper changes, not the model

points.v: Model identifiers, version strings, and regional availability differ per route
Inference profiles
Model deployments
Model Garden access controls

quiz.q: An engineer copies a working configuration between two cloud environments and the calls fail immediately, even though the same model is offered in both. What differs?
options: The model is a genuinely different build on each cloud and therefore requires every prompt to be re-tuned.
Nothing at all should differ between them, so the failure must be a network or a credential problem.
Identifiers, version strings, and regional availability differ, and each route wraps access differently — inference profiles, model deployments, Model Garden controls.
Only the region names differ; model identifiers and version strings are fully standardized across all four routes.
quiz.why: Across routes the wrapper changes, not the model: Bedrock uses inference profiles, Foundry model deployments, Vertex Model Garden access controls, and identifiers and version strings differ.

items.sourceSection: Security, governance, and regulated-industry constraints
items.lead: Compliance constraints rule entry points in or out before cost/build effort

points.v: Attorney-client privilege, HIPAA, GDPR, FedRAMP, or data-residency policy make this call
Eliminated most often — consumer-grade, not designed for every enterprise data-handling requirement
With logging, retention, and identity controls in the partner's own infrastructure — survives most regulated reviews

quiz.q: A law firm bound by privilege and a data-residency policy asks which way of consuming Claude survives its compliance review, and which is usually ruled out first.
options: The consumer web product is usually eliminated; API and SDK behind the partner's own gateway, with logging, retention, and identity controls, survives.
Cost and build effort decide the matter first of all; the compliance constraints are then applied afterwards to whatever has already been chosen.
The API is ruled out because traffic leaves the firm's network; the consumer product with enterprise SSO survives review.
Every available option fails here; regulated firms of this kind simply cannot use hosted models at any tier whatsoever.
quiz.why: Compliance constraints rule entry points in or out before cost or build effort. Claude.ai is eliminated most often as consumer-grade; API plus SDK via a partner gateway survives.

items.topic: Compliance must not run on subagents
items.sourceSection: The annotation across the diagram

points.v: The highest-consequence path must run in deterministic server-side code, not on subagents — subagents provide weaker deterministic guarantees

items.logic: Giving a compliance subagent its own restricted tool entry point looks safe and modular, but narrowing tools doesn't make subagent execution deterministic.

quiz.q: A design puts the sanctions-screening step in a dedicated subagent with a deliberately narrow tool set, arguing that the narrow scope is what makes it safe. Verdict?
options: Sound — restricting the tool set narrowly is precisely what makes that screening step deterministic.
Sound, provided the subagent is pinned to the most capable model tier that is available.
Unsound, but only because a subagent adds unacceptable latency to what is a synchronous screening path.
Unsound — the highest-consequence path must run in deterministic server-side code; subagents give weaker deterministic guarantees.
quiz.why: Narrowing a subagent's tools does not make its execution deterministic. The highest-consequence path belongs in deterministic server-side code, not on subagents.

items.sourceSection: Glossary
items.lead: Claude Code is distributed across four channels

points.v: CLI
IDE plugins (VS Code, JetBrains, and others)
Desktop application
Web product at claude.ai/code

quiz.q: A rollout plan assumes the coding tool is terminal-only, so machines without shell access are excluded from the pilot entirely. Is that assumption correct?
options: Yes; the terminal really is the only channel through which that product ships to customers today.
No — it also ships as IDE plugins, a desktop application, and a web product at claude.ai/code.
No — it also ships as a browser extension and a companion mobile application for phones.
Yes, unless the organisation separately licenses the differently branded enterprise edition of the same tool.
quiz.why: Claude Code is distributed across four channels: CLI, IDE plugins (VS Code, JetBrains, and others), a desktop application, and the web product at claude.ai/code.

items.topic: Five factors that pick the pattern
items.sourceSection: Key takeaways
items.lead: Five factors decide among augmented LLM, workflow, and agent

points.v: Predictability
Error cost
Observability
Latency
Cost
The tightest/binding constraint decides the pattern

quiz.q: A team lists everything that matters for a new build and asks how to turn that list into a choice between a single augmented call, a fixed pipeline, or a model-driven loop.
options: Score each option against all of the criteria and simply pick the highest weighted total.
Start with the most flexible option and simplify only if the cost later becomes a problem.
Weigh predictability, error cost, observability, latency, and cost — the tightest binding constraint decides.
Let error cost decide alone; every other factor is a downstream consequence of it anyway.
quiz.why: Five factors decide among augmented LLM, workflow, and agent: predictability, error cost, observability, latency, cost. The binding constraint decides, not an aggregate score.

items.sourceSection: Key takeaways
items.lead: The five tested reference architectures are exactly these

points.v: Agent
RAG
Document processing pipeline (Evaluator-optimizer)
Routing
Coding agent

quiz.q: An architect is asked which tested starting points already exist, before anyone designs something bespoke for the client. Which set is it?
options: Agent, RAG, document processing pipeline (evaluator-optimizer), routing, and coding agent.
Agent, RAG, prompt chaining, parallelization, and the classic orchestrator-worker coordination pattern.
RAG, fine-tuning, routing, prompt caching, and asynchronous batch processing.
Agent, multi-agent system, workflow, augmented LLM, and coding agent.
quiz.why: The five tested reference architectures are exactly agent, RAG, document processing pipeline (evaluator-optimizer), routing, and coding agent — a fixed list, distinct from pattern names.

items.sourceSection: The four properties architects design around / Sources
items.lead: Four properties, distinct from the four design consequences they map to

points.v: Next-token prediction
Knowledge
"The property with the hardest edge" — inside the window attention is available, outside it there is no access at all
Steerability

quiz.q: An architect explains that one of the model's underlying characteristics is all-or-nothing: full access on one side of a boundary, none at all beyond it. Which one, and its companions?
options: Knowledge — alongside non-determinism, context as a finite resource, and confidence is not validity.
Steerability — alongside next-token prediction, knowledge, and working memory as its three companions.
Context as a finite resource — alongside each of the other three design consequences.
Working memory — with its three companions being next-token prediction, knowledge, and steerability.
quiz.why: The four properties are next-token prediction, knowledge, working memory, and steerability. Working memory has the hardest edge: inside the window attention is available, outside it there is none.

items.sourceSection: Where Claude fits (Claude / systems / humans)

points.v: What Claude does, what existing systems do, and what humans do
AI-appropriate work, human-retained work, collaborative work (Claude drafts, a person decides)

quiz.q: One section of a design doc divides the work three ways; another section divides it three ways again, differently. A reviewer calls this a duplication error. Is it?
options: Yes; the doc simply repeats one split with inconsistent wording, and the two ought to be merged together.
No — the second split is simply the first one restated after the three tests have been applied.
No — one split is owner buckets (Claude, existing systems, humans); the other is delegation-map categories (AI-appropriate, human-retained, collaborative).
Yes; only the delegation-map categories form a real taxonomy, so the other one ought to be deleted entirely.
quiz.why: Two distinct three-way splits exist: owner buckets — what Claude does, what existing systems do, what humans do — and the delegation map's AI-appropriate, human-retained, and collaborative work.

items.sourceSection: When retrieval got reached for instead of a tool call

points.v: "Context engineering" is reserved for deciding which mechanism is responsible for getting each kind of data in front of the model; retrieval over a vector index is only one such mechanism

quiz.q: A team claims to have covered how data reaches the model, pointing to its vector index and embedding model as the entire scope of that work. What is missing?
options: Nothing at all is missing; a well-tuned vector index really is the complete answer for getting any data to the model reliably.
The scope is deciding which mechanism is responsible for each kind of data; retrieval over an index is only one mechanism.
A larger embedding model, which is ultimately what determines how much of the data actually reaches the model.
Only the chunking strategy is missing; index tuning otherwise covers the whole of that discipline already.
quiz.why: Context engineering is reserved for deciding which mechanism gets each kind of data in front of the model. Retrieval over a vector index is one mechanism among several.

items.sourceSection: The most common mistake: retrieval applied to live state

points.v: Stale chunks, results shifting with each index refresh, answers contradicting the database
Not a better embedding model or shorter refresh interval — call the system that owns the live state
High — the system looks healthy: normal latency, no errors

items.logic: Stale or contradictory results look like a retrieval-quality problem, but no refresh interval makes an index a source of live state.

quiz.q: Answers contradict the database, results shift after each index refresh, and latency and error rates look entirely normal. The team is trialling better embedding models. What is the fix?
options: Call the system that owns the live state; no refresh interval makes an index a source of live state.
A much shorter refresh interval, so that the index tracks the underlying source system far more closely.
A stronger embedding model plus a reranker, which together resolve the contradictions the users are seeing.
A confidence threshold, so that contradictory chunks are suppressed before any answer is composed for the user.
quiz.why: This is retrieval applied to live state. The fix is not a better embedding model or a shorter refresh interval; detection cost is high because latency and errors look normal.

items.sourceSection: How to decide if a problem needs one or several patterns

points.v: Reach for a second reference architecture only when the two parts of the problem break in different ways worth managing separately
Reaching for one because you haven't decided what problem you're solving is "a design decision you're deferring, not a pattern you're applying"
Composing roughly doubles the surface area to maintain — when in doubt, pick one

quiz.q: A proposal stacks two reference architectures because the team has not yet settled what the product actually does. What should the architect call this, and what is the rule?
options: Sensible hedging; composing simply keeps all of the options open until the product requirements have properly firmed up later on in delivery.
A required step; every serious production system ends up composing at least two reference architectures anyway.
A cost problem only; composition adds spend but no extra maintenance surface that is worth worrying about.
A deferred design decision, not a pattern; compose only when the two parts break in different ways worth managing separately.
quiz.why: Reaching for a second architecture because you haven't decided what problem you're solving is a design decision you're deferring. Composing roughly doubles maintenance surface — when in doubt, pick one.

items.topic: Guardrails belong in the output contract
items.sourceSection: Author the reusable prompt asset

points.v: Enforce a guardrail structurally by building it into the output contract as a constraint the format requires, not as a sentence in the role text
"A rule stated in the role can be drifted past. A constraint built into the output contract shapes the response format and cannot be quietly ignored."

items.logic: A forcefully worded prohibition in the role section reads like a real guardrail, but an instruction the model can route around is not a constraint.

quiz.q: A prompt's role section states in bold that the assistant must never give financial advice, yet advice still slips through occasionally. How should the rule be enforced?
options: Strengthen the wording and repeat the prohibition again at the very end of the prompt.
Build it into the output contract as a constraint the format itself requires.
Move it into the user message, where the model weights instructions rather more heavily.
Add a post-hoc classifier and accept that prompt-level enforcement is simply impossible here.
quiz.why: A rule stated in the role text can be drifted past. A constraint built into the output contract shapes the response format and cannot be quietly ignored.

items.sourceSection: Designing system prompts, templates, and guardrails

points.v: An underspecified guardrail is worse than a missing one, "because it creates the appearance of a control without the substance"
Underspecification — a gap the model fills with its own assumption, differently each time — is the named key failure in prompt design

items.logic: Partial protection seems strictly better than none, but the appearance of a control stops anyone from adding the real one.

quiz.q: A reviewer finds a safety rule that covers only some cases and leaves the rest to the model's own assumption. A colleague argues partial coverage still beats nothing at all.
options: The colleague is right; any amount of partial coverage strictly reduces the overall risk relative to having no rule at all.
The colleague is right, provided the remaining gap is clearly documented somewhere in the team's design doc.
The colleague is wrong: this is worse than a missing rule, creating the appearance of a control without the substance.
Neither point really matters; rules stated at the prompt layer have no measurable effect on behaviour either way.
quiz.why: Underspecification — a gap the model fills with its own assumption each time — is the named key failure in prompt design; the appearance of control blocks the real one.

items.sourceSection: Avoiding bias in prompt construction
items.lead: Prompt bias enters through three sources, answered by three disciplines

points.v: Fix: phrase neutrally
Fix: balance examples across the cases the system will see
Fix: check whether the prompt presumes the answer it should elicit
Bias is invisible in any single output and shows only in aggregate — a design requirement, not a polish step

quiz.q: A hiring-screen prompt produces defensible outputs whenever anyone spot-checks it, yet aggregate outcomes skew against one group. Where does the problem enter, and how is it caught?
options: Through leading phrasing, unbalanced examples, and assumptions baked into instructions; it shows only in aggregate.
Through model non-determinism; it is caught by simply re-running each prompt several times over.
Through the training data alone; nothing in prompt construction can introduce or remove it.
Through the temperature setting; it is caught by spot-checking individual outputs far more often.
quiz.why: Prompt bias enters via leading phrasing, unbalanced examples, and assumptions baked into instructions. It is invisible in any single output and shows only in aggregate — a design requirement.

items.sourceSection: What extended thinking controls

points.v: Run evals without extended thinking first; consider enabling it only if accuracy still misses requirements after working on the prompt

items.logic: It looks like a free quality upgrade, but without measured evidence you pay thinking tokens and latency on every call with no proof it moves accuracy.

quiz.q: Before a single eval has been run, a team enables the extra reasoning pass on every endpoint, calling it a free quality upgrade. What is the recommended order?
options: Enable it first and then measure — it never lowers accuracy, so the measurement can wait.
Run evals without it first; consider enabling it only if accuracy still misses requirements after prompt work.
Enable it only on the slowest requests, where its added latency cost is already being absorbed anyway.
Enable it everywhere but set the lowest effort level, which removes the need for any eval evidence.
quiz.why: Without measured evidence, extended thinking costs thinking tokens and latency on every call. Run evals without it first; enable only if accuracy still misses after prompt work.

items.topic: MCP exposes tools, prompts, and resources
items.sourceSection: Glossary

points.v: An MCP server exposes tools, prompts, AND resources that any MCP-compatible client can use, so one integration written once is reused across applications — shifting tool-definition maintenance out of application code and into reusable servers

quiz.q: A team assumes the protocol server it is building can only publish callable functions, so it duplicates its reference documents into each consuming application. What has it missed?
options: Nothing at all; only callable functions are ever shareable this way, so the duplication really is unavoidable.
The documents belong in a vector index instead, because such servers simply cannot host any content.
The server can also expose prompts and resources, so one integration is written once and reused everywhere.
Servers can expose resources but not prompts, so the prompt duplication does remain necessary here.
quiz.why: An MCP server exposes tools, prompts, and resources to any MCP-compatible client, shifting tool-definition maintenance out of application code and into reusable servers.

items.sourceSection: The grading ladder: choosing how to grade

points.v: Wherever behavior allows — schema validation, exact match, length, presence checks
When behavior needs interpretation
Last resort — reserved for high-stakes or novel behaviors neither code nor a calibrated judge can trust

quiz.q: A team's eval suite routes every single check to a human reviewer, including 'is the JSON parseable' and 'is the reply under 500 characters'. Throughput has collapsed and the backlog grows daily. What is wrong?
options: Human review is the correct default for a compliance-facing suite; it simply needs more reviewers staffed.
Those checks are deterministic, so they belong in code; human grading is the last resort.
Route every check through an LLM judge instead, since judges scale better than people.
Schema and length checks belong to an LLM judge; humans should keep the rest.
quiz.why: The grading ladder puts code-based checks first, LLM-as-judge for interpretation, humans last. Staffing more reviewers scales the wrong rung of the ladder.

items.sourceSection: The grading ladder: choosing how to grade

points.v: Detailed, not vague
Small fixed label set, not free-form scores
Against human-labeled examples
Judge must differ from the model being evaluated, to avoid self-preference
An uncalibrated judge is worse than no automated grade — it appears trustworthy but isn't

quiz.q: A summarization system is scored by asking the same model that wrote the summaries to 'rate the quality from 1 to 10'. Nobody has compared those numbers to human labels. Reviewers ask why the 8.7 average shouldn't be trusted.
options: The scores are usable; a 1-10 scale gives more resolution than a fixed label set.
The sample is too small; run the same judge across many more summaries.
Vague rubric, free-form scores, no calibration, and the model is grading its own output.
Swap in the strongest available model as the judge and the numbers become reliable.
quiz.why: LLM-as-judge rigor requires a detailed rubric, constrained verdicts, calibration against human labels, and a different model. Scaling an uncalibrated judge just multiplies untrustworthy scores.

items.sourceSection: Defining success criteria: turning a business requirement into a measurable threshold

points.v: Specify exactly what behavior is being measured
From the business requirement, not from what the first prototype achieves
Name the ways it can fail
Add inputs designed to break it

quiz.q: A client says the assistant must never misquote policy. The team turns that into a check using the twelve prompts from the demo and a pass bar of 91%, the number the prototype happened to score.
options: Set the threshold from the business requirement, name the failure modes, add adversarial inputs.
Ninety-one percent is defensible precisely because the prototype demonstrably achieves it today.
Raise the bar to one hundred percent; anything lower is not a real criterion.
Twelve prompts suffice as long as a human carefully reviews each one every run.
quiz.why: Requirement-to-criterion mapping takes the threshold from the business requirement, not from the first prototype's score, and requires named failure modes plus adversarial inputs.

items.sourceSection: Evals as the gating mechanism for change

points.v: Evals present but out of date carry higher regression risk than no evals at all

items.logic: Any eval suite seems strictly safer than none, but a stale one silently passes changes by measuring behavior the system no longer has.

quiz.q: Three teams ship the same prompt change. Team A has nothing automated. Team B's checks match current behavior. Team C's checks were written for a prompt two rewrites ago and still come back green. Who carries the most regression risk?
options: Team A — having any eval suite at all is strictly safer than having none.
Team C — a stale suite passes while measuring behavior the system no longer has.
Team B — a passing suite breeds false confidence no matter how fresh it is.
Teams A and C equally, since neither has a suite reflecting the current prompt.
quiz.why: Evals present but out of date carry higher regression risk than no evals: the green result silently certifies behavior the system has already stopped having.

items.sourceSection: From POC to production: cost, latency, and reliability
items.lead: All four dimensions are invisible in a demo

points.v: Cost
Latency
Reliability
Failure modes

quiz.q: A pilot ran fifty hand-picked requests through a notebook and impressed the client in a demo. The delivery lead asks what still stands between that result and committing to a production build.
options: Model choice, prompt wording, interface polish, and end-user documentation.
Nothing substantive; the notebook's behavior transfers directly at production scale.
Security review alone, since the technical behavior is already demonstrated.
Cost, latency, reliability, and failure modes.
