quiz.why: The POC-to-production gap is cost, latency, reliability, and failure modes. A demo on fifty curated requests demonstrates none of them, so 'it already works' fails.

items.sourceSection: Cost and latency modeling: Know the numbers before you build

points.v: A cost model built on average token usage can underestimate long-tail request cost by a factor of 2-3, since most requests are short but a tail consumes a disproportionate share of spend

items.logic: Sizing off observed average token count feels sound, but the average hides a tail that can double or triple real cost.

quiz.q: You sized a contract-review deployment by multiplying daily call volume by the mean token count from a two-week sample. Three months in, finance reports spend running far above the forecast.
options: The mean token count was a sound basis for sizing; the daily volume estimate must be wrong.
Output tokens were left out of the calculation, which understates every request equally.
Most requests are short, but a long tail consumes disproportionate spend — two to three times.
Published token prices changed between the sampling window and the deployment date.
quiz.why: Average-based cost models hide a long tail that underestimates cost by two to three times. Blaming volume leaves the same flawed average driving the forecast.

items.sourceSection: Cost and latency modeling: Know the numbers before you build

points.v: ~10% of the standard input token rate (verify current rate at platform.claude.com/docs)

quiz.q: A finance stakeholder is building a savings model and asks what a token served from a stored prefix costs relative to an ordinary one.
options: Roughly half the standard input rate, so caching halves the input line item.
Roughly ten percent of the standard input token rate.
Nothing at all — tokens served from cache are not billed.
The same as the standard input rate; caching buys latency, not cost.
quiz.why: Cache reads price at roughly 10% of the standard input rate; modeling them as free or half-price gives the client a forecast the invoice contradicts.

items.sourceSection: Reliability controls: what to build into every model call

points.v: Exponential backoff, placed close to the API call
At the service boundary
To a different model tier or cached response, in the orchestration layer
A control in the wrong layer leaves the right part exposed; fallback behavior must be tested as part of the eval suite

quiz.q: During an upstream incident, requests retried but the whole service still hung, and there was no degraded path for users. The team is now deciding where each of its protective mechanisms should sit.
options: Backoff retries next to the API call, circuit breakers at the service boundary, fallbacks in orchestration.
All three belong in the orchestration layer, so that every failure path lives in exactly one place.
All three inside the API client, since that is where the failures actually originate.
Retries at the service boundary, breakers in orchestration, fallbacks beside the API call.
quiz.why: Reliability controls each belong in a specific layer — one in the wrong layer leaves the right part exposed. Centralizing all three leaves the call site unprotected.

items.sourceSection: Failure modes by architecture type
items.lead: Applies equally to every architecture type — an operational discipline

points.v: In configuration
The Anthropic model deprecation page
Maintain a version-update runbook

quiz.q: A production integration references an alias that resolves to whatever the current model is. Overnight the outputs shifted noticeably and nobody on the team knew anything had changed.
options: Add retries so behavior changes introduced by a new version are absorbed automatically.
Re-run the eval suite weekly; pinning is unnecessary while the evals stay green.
Pin the version in configuration, monitor the deprecation page, keep an update runbook.
Freeze permanently on this model and disregard the vendor's deprecation notices.
quiz.why: Version pinning lives in configuration, paired with deprecation monitoring and a version-update runbook. Weekly evals only detect the change after users have already met it.

items.sourceSection: How to size a use case

points.v: Explicit marker required in the request to enable prompt caching
Cost more per token than standard input
5 minutes — workloads with request frequency lower than this won't see consistent caching savings

quiz.q: An integration sends an identical 25k-token preamble several times a minute and the team expected the savings to appear on their own. Input spend is flat, and the one experiment they tried briefly raised the bill.
options: An explicit marker is required on the reused block, and writes bill above standard input.
A preamble of twenty-five thousand tokens exceeds the maximum size any prefix is allowed to reuse.
Savings apply to output tokens, so a long shared input prefix cannot help.
The mechanism switches on automatically once ten identical requests have been observed.
quiz.why: Prompt caching needs an explicit cache_control marker in the request; cache writes cost more per token than standard input, explaining the brief rise. Nothing activates automatically.

items.sourceSection: How to size a use case
items.lead: For workloads whose SLA permits async processing

points.v: 50% price reduction vs standard API pricing
Up to 100,000 requests per batch
For regulated workloads, verify BAA/compliance coverage before routing PHI through batch

quiz.q: A hospital analytics group wants to halve spend on an overnight job of 80,000 summarization requests over patient records. Nothing about the job is latency-sensitive.
options: Batch is unusable here: the per-batch ceiling is ten thousand requests.
Batch gives a fifty percent reduction and is automatically covered by any BAA the customer signed.
Batch discounts apply only to output tokens, so a summarization job gains little.
Batch fits — fifty percent off, under the 100,000 limit — but verify BAA coverage for PHI.
quiz.why: The Batch API gives a 50% reduction and takes up to 100,000 requests per batch; assuming BAA coverage carries over routes PHI through an unverified configuration.

items.sourceSection: How to scope a use case
items.lead: Four ordered steps, each building on the last

points.v: Business requirement → capability list
Capability list → architecture sketch
Architecture sketch → boundary conditions
Boundary conditions → scope in the SOW (statement of work)

quiz.q: A delivery team drafted the statement of work straight from the client's stated business goal. Mid-build they discover load limits and input-size ceilings nobody priced. What ordering should they have followed?
options: Business requirement straight to boundary conditions, then architecture, then the capability list.
Architecture sketch first, since architecture determines which capabilities are even possible.
The SOW should be written first so the agreed budget constrains the architecture.
Requirement to capability list, to architecture sketch, to boundary conditions, to SOW scope.
quiz.why: The scoping sequence derives boundary conditions from the architecture sketch, which derives from the capability list; jumping straight to the SOW skips the step that surfaces them.

items.sourceSection: Business value and ROI mapping: turning a feasible design into a justified investment

points.v: A 'feasible with constraints' verdict whose constraints aren't documented becomes an infeasible system the moment those constraints are violated in production; documented constraints carry the same design weight as the architecture itself

items.logic: Once the demo works, 'feasible with constraints' feels equivalent to plain 'feasible' and writing the constraints down feels like paperwork.

quiz.q: A pilot succeeds provided inputs stay under 40 pages and traffic below two requests per second. The team reports the assessment as a success and moves to build without recording either bound anywhere.
options: Acceptable — the demo worked, so the verdict is effectively 'feasible'; writing bounds down is paperwork.
Acceptable if the bounds are mentioned verbally to the client's engineering lead.
Those bounds are load-bearing design constraints; unwritten, the system becomes infeasible once violated.
The bounds should be engineered away rather than documented, since documentation ages badly.
quiz.why: 'Feasible with constraints' carries its constraints with the same design weight as the architecture. Treating it as plain 'feasible' fails the moment production violates them.

items.sourceSection: Business value and ROI mapping: turning a feasible design into a justified investment

points.v: Same work faster or cheaper
Work not feasible before becoming possible
More output from the same people
The run cost of the system
The service levels the deployment must hold

quiz.q: An executive sponsor asks how the deployment's value will be argued at the annual review. The team has prepared only a cost-per-call figure.
options: Accuracy, latency, throughput, uptime, and user satisfaction.
Efficiency, transformation, productivity, solution cost, and performance SLAs.
Build cost, run cost, headcount saved, and annual license fees.
Cost per call is the entire value case; the rest is marketing framing.
quiz.why: The five ROI pillars include transformation and performance SLAs alongside cost. A purely technical metric list omits the value the sponsor is actually being asked to fund.

items.sourceSection: Business value and ROI mapping: turning a feasible design into a justified investment
items.lead: Four steps once a design is feasible with constraints

points.v: Name the baseline in a business unit, using the business owner's own operational data
The post-deployment state in that unit, including any human-review cost the feasibility verdict requires
From the sizing model — recurring cost only; build cost is accounted separately
State the payback period and its sensitivity to volume and gain-per-task assumptions
Time for accumulated operational gain to cover build cost plus run cost

quiz.q: A value case uses an industry benchmark for today's handling time, omits the reviewer the feasibility verdict requires, and subtracts the build cost from the first year's gain.
options: Sound — an industry benchmark is far more objective than one business unit's messy operational data.
Baseline on the owner's own data, include required review cost, subtract recurring run cost, state payback.
Replace the benchmark with the prototype's measured latency and leave everything else as is.
Drop the payback period, since it rests on volume assumptions nobody can know yet.
quiz.why: ROI mapping baselines on the business owner's operational data and subtracts recurring run cost only — build cost is accounted separately, so subtracting it double-counts.

items.sourceSection: What went wrong (The scoping call that skipped the constraints)

points.v: Convert daily call volume into an average inter-request interval before concluding parallelization is needed — at a low enough rate, sequential processing meets even a tight latency SLA; volume pressures cost, not latency
Task complexity, model size, output length

items.logic: High daily volume plus a tight per-request latency SLA looks like it demands concurrent request-handling infrastructure.

quiz.q: A client processes 8,000 documents a day, spread evenly across 24 hours, and each result must return within 20 seconds. The architect proposes a concurrent worker pool to meet the deadline.
options: Justified — that daily volume with a tight per-request SLA demands concurrent request handling.
Convert volume into an average inter-request interval first; sequential processing may meet the SLA.
Justified — latency is driven by call volume, so concurrency is the only available lever.
Unnecessary, because latency requirements never influence architecture; only cost pressure does.
quiz.why: Volume pressures cost, not latency — latency comes from task complexity, model size, and output length. Assuming volume forces concurrency buys infrastructure the SLA never needed.

items.sourceSection: What went wrong

points.v: Handles a 300-page contract without chunking
May require chunking for the longest documents
Context window capacity is part of the model tier decision, not a settled assumption

quiz.q: A legal client's core workload is 300-page contracts that must be analyzed whole. The team assumes a splitting pipeline is unavoidable and prices several weeks of extra engineering for it.
options: Correct — no model available today handles a document of that size in a single pass.
Splitting is always preferable anyway, because it reduces total token spend.
A 200k-token window removes any need for splitting, even on the longest documents.
Window capacity is part of the tier choice: a 1M-token window fits it whole.
quiz.why: Context window capacity belongs to the model tier decision, not a settled assumption; a 200k window may still require chunking, while a 1M window handles 300 pages whole.

items.sourceSection: What went wrong (The scoping call that skipped the constraints)
items.lead: Gather these three before issuing any feasibility verdict

points.v: Call volume
Input size
Latency requirement

quiz.q: A scoping call ends with the client's goal and desired accuracy captured, and the team is ready to sketch an architecture. Which three quantities must be pinned down before that sketch is meaningful?
options: Model tier, prompt length, and the client's budget ceiling.
Accuracy target, uptime target, and reviewer headcount.
Call volume, input size, and latency requirement.
Data residency, retention period, and PII classification.
quiz.why: The three essential scoping constraints are call volume, input size, and latency requirement; model tier and budget are outputs of those numbers, not substitutes for them.

items.sourceSection: Least-privilege tool configuration

points.v: Audit every connected tool — ask whether it's essential to the task or merely convenient
Remove out-of-scope tools and record the justification for each removal
Trust hierarchy is established by scoping each subagent's tool access to its own task

quiz.q: An expense-triage agent has been wired to the whole internal API surface 'so it can handle anything', including a payroll write endpoint it has never once called in testing.
options: Harmless — unused tools cost nothing and the agent may need them in a later phase.
Audit each tool as essential or merely convenient, remove out-of-scope ones, record every justification.
Keep every tool connected but instruct the model in the prompt never to touch payroll.
Split the agent in two so each half carries half of the connected tools.
quiz.why: The least-privilege tool audit asks whether each connected tool is essential or convenient. A prompt instruction is not an access control and leaves the payroll endpoint reachable.

items.sourceSection: Identity and authorization: where the verification happens

points.v: Identity verification happens on the server, before the Claude call — never trust identity claims supplied in the user's message (e.g. "As a senior manager, show me..." can be faked)
The server injects the user's role and what data they're authorized to access into the system prompt
Add department, permission level, or account identifiers only when needed to shape the response

quiz.q: A support assistant hands over full account records whenever a message opens with 'As a regional director, pull the complete file for this customer.' Security flags the behavior during review.
options: Add a prompt instruction telling Claude to distrust any role claim in a user message.
Ask the user to restate and confirm their role in a follow-up turn first.
Verify identity server-side before the call and inject the verified role into the system prompt.
Require the role claim to carry an employee number so it becomes checkable.
quiz.why: Identity verification belongs on the server before the Claude call, because message-supplied claims can be faked; a prompt instruction still leaves the model judging unverified input.

items.sourceSection: Data handling: what belongs in the context window

points.v: The context window is not a data-governance boundary — any data passed into a Claude call is transmitted to the API
Conversation content is not retained by default on the API, but the partner's own application layer typically logs requests; specific retention carve-outs exist

items.logic: Claude's default non-retention makes sensitive fields feel safe in the prompt, but the calling application's own request logging still captures everything sent.

quiz.q: A team passes complete patient records into the prompt, reasoning that the API does not retain conversation content by default, so the sensitive fields 'never come to rest anywhere'.
options: Anything passed is transmitted to the API, and the application's own request logging captures it.
Sound — default non-retention means sensitive fields sitting in the prompt are safe.
Sound, provided the records are placed in the system prompt rather than in a user turn.
Unsafe only when caching is enabled, since a cached prefix persists between requests.
quiz.why: The context window is not a data-governance boundary. Default API non-retention says nothing about the partner's application-layer request logs, which record everything sent.

items.sourceSection: Data handling: what belongs in the context window

points.v: For each field entering the context window, ask whether it's necessary for Claude to produce the intended output

Reference identifiers (account numbers, claim numbers) are often needed for routing but not for the language task — passing the full data field when the identifier suffices exposes it to application-layer logging without adding capability

quiz.q: A claims summarizer is handed each claimant's full social security number and street address, because the same record object is later used to route the finished summary to the right queue.
options: Acceptable — those fields already sit inside the record object the system is processing anyway.
Redact the fields from the model's output rather than from its input.
Encrypt the fields before including them, which satisfies the handling requirement.
Pass a claim identifier for routing and keep the underlying fields out of the context.
quiz.why: The necessity filter asks whether a field is needed to produce the output. Routing needs only the identifier; the full fields add application-log exposure without adding capability.

items.sourceSection: Observability: what to log, what to trace, and why

points.v: Model version, input token count, prompt identifier
Output token count, latency, stop reason
User role, session ID, whether caching was applied
Whether the downstream system accepted the output, plus any rejection signals

quiz.q: A postmortem stalls. Nobody can tell which prompt version served the bad responses, whether the stored prefix was hit, or whether the downstream system accepted the outputs at all.
options: Log request, response, context, and outcome — including prompt identifier, caching flag, acceptance signal.
Log the complete prompt text and complete response text for every single request that runs.
Log only errors, since successful requests carry no diagnostic value later.
Log latency and token counts; everything else is reconstructable from the model version.
quiz.why: The four logging categories are request, response, context, and outcome. Storing raw prompt and response text still omits the caching flag and the downstream acceptance signal.

items.sourceSection: Observability: what to log, what to trace, and why

points.v: Without a trustworthy audit trail, an autonomous system is not approved to act — security reviewers treat observability as the precondition for enabling agents, and an agentic action taken but not logged is treated as one that cannot be allowed

quiz.q: A security review refuses to let an autonomous scheduling agent take actions on its own. The team objects that it scored 98% in testing and that its guardrails are strict.
options: The block is unjustified; measured accuracy is the criterion that should govern approval.
Approval needs documented human sign-off on every action, which no amount of logging can replace.
Approval requires a trustworthy audit trail; an action taken but not logged cannot be allowed.
The block lifts automatically once the agent's tools are reduced to read-only calls.
quiz.why: Observability is the precondition reviewers set for enabling agents — an agentic action taken but not logged is treated as one that cannot be allowed. Accuracy doesn't substitute.

items.sourceSection: Observability: what to log, what to trace, and why

points.v: Separate API keys per tenant are required for attribution and isolation in any production multi-tenant deployment — on a shared key, an org-level rate-limit breach is visible but can't be attributed to the tenant that caused it, and every tenant absorbs the impact

quiz.q: A SaaS platform serves thirty customers through a single shared credential. One customer's traffic surge trips an org-level limit, every customer goes down, and nobody can prove which one caused it.
options: Raise the organization's rate limit and add client-side throttling for each customer.
Add a tenant identifier to the request body so the logs can attribute the traffic.
Separate API keys per tenant, which production multi-tenant deployments require.
Shard customers by region so each region's traffic consumes a different limit.
quiz.why: Per-tenant API keys give attribution and isolation. A tenant ID in the payload labels your own logs, but the limit stays shared, so every tenant still absorbs the breach.

items.sourceSection: Observability: what to log, what to trace, and why

points.v: Retroactive PII redaction across a log history never designed to support it is the most expensive data-handling fix in a production Claude system
An integration without PII redaction prior to the API call exposes sensitive fields to application-layer request logging on every request

quiz.q: An integration has been live two years, sending raw customer records to the API with no scrubbing beforehand. Legal now demands the entire historical request log be cleaned.
options: Routine cleanup work — a straightforward log-processing job resolves the whole thing within one sprint.
Retroactive redaction across a log history never designed for it: the most expensive fix.
Delete the entire log history, which costs nothing and satisfies the demand.
The exposure is output-side; redact model responses before they reach storage.
quiz.why: Retroactive PII redaction over a log history never designed to support it is the most expensive data-handling fix; the exposure came from skipping redaction before the API call.

items.sourceSection: Reading results without overclaiming

points.v: LLM experiments have a failure mode classical A/B tests don't: interaction effects between the treatment and specific input types — a prompt change that improves typical inputs can degrade rare edge cases that appear frequently in a later seasonal spike
Test-period and input-distribution alignment matter more here than in most other software contexts

quiz.q: A prompt change tested in July improved every measured metric on live traffic and shipped. In November complaints spike on a request type that was rare during the test window.
options: A statistical fluke — the July result reached significance and therefore still holds.
The model has drifted; re-running the identical July test will confirm the regression.
Treatment can interact with input type — a case rare in testing became common later.
The July measurement window was too short; extend the same test to a full quarter.
quiz.why: LLM experiments carry interaction effects between treatment and specific input types, unlike classical A/B tests, so input-distribution alignment matters. Model drift is a different cause entirely.

items.sourceSection: Shadow testing: validating a change before any user sees it

points.v: Use when deployment can absorb small bounded exposure to a worse version and traffic is high enough for a meaningful sample in a reasonable window
Use when a single bad output carries too much risk or traffic is too low to split

Shadow testing costs downstream signal — scoring relies on an offline rubric or golden answers rather than real user behavior — and is often the only acceptable validation method in regulated-industry deployments

quiz.q: A regulated insurer's underwriting assistant handles 200 requests a day, and a single wrong recommendation reaching a customer is unacceptable. How should the next prompt revision be validated?
options: Live A/B on five percent of traffic, since a small slice bounds the risk adequately.
Live A/B regardless, because only real user behavior produces trustworthy scores.
Ship to all traffic and watch complaints, which is faster than either split design.
Shadow testing scored against golden answers or an offline rubric, accepting lost live signal.
quiz.why: Shadow testing suits cases where one bad output is too risky or traffic too low to split; even a five percent live split exposes real customers to the worse version.

items.sourceSection: Observability at scale: instrumentation design, dashboards, anomaly detection

points.v: Request-level tracing
Metric aggregation
Anomaly detection
Change attribution

quiz.q: Leadership wants one stack that can answer, at any moment, what the system is doing, how well it is performing, when its behavior shifted, and why it shifted. Which four mechanisms deliver that?
options: Request-level tracing, metric aggregation, anomaly detection, and change attribution.
Dashboards, alerting, an on-call rotation, and written postmortems.
Logging, monitoring, distributed tracing, and continuous profiling.
Unit tests, integration tests, eval suites, and A/B experiments.
quiz.why: The four observability questions map to tracing, metric aggregation, anomaly detection, and change attribution. Generic ops rituals such as postmortems answer none of the four directly.

items.sourceSection: Observability at scale: instrumentation design, dashboards, anomaly detection

points.v: >150% of the 7-day average deserves an alert
Crossing the SLA threshold deserves an alert
Hard to catch with threshold alerts — needs periodic distribution comparison instead

quiz.q: An SRE wants three alarms on the Claude integration: one for runaway spend, one for slow responses, and one for the model behaving differently on inputs that have not changed.
options: Spend over 150% of the 7-day average, p95 latency crossing the SLA, drift by distribution comparison.
All three as static thresholds, retuned monthly against the previous month's peak.
Spend over 300% of yesterday's total, p50 latency above one second, and drift above five percent.
Only spend and latency are alertable; behavioral drift cannot be detected at all.
quiz.why: Cost spikes alert above 150% of the 7-day average and latency on p95 against the SLA, but model drift resists threshold alerts and needs periodic distribution comparison instead.

items.sourceSection: Observability at scale: instrumentation design, dashboards, anomaly detection

points.v: Behavior on stable inputs changed
The input distribution changed
The version changed and behaves differently on existing inputs
Mixing them up produces the wrong fix

quiz.q: Output quality dropped last week. The team cannot tell whether the incoming requests changed, the model behaves differently on the same requests, or a new version landed — and each fix they try misses.
options: These are all the same underlying phenomenon under different names; any of the fixes will work.
Model drift, data drift, and model update effects are distinct; conflating them misdirects the fix.
Only a rollback can distinguish them, so roll back before investigating anything else.
Rewrite the prompt first, since prompt failure explains all three observed patterns.
quiz.why: Change attribution separates model drift, data drift, and model update effects; treating them as one phenomenon aims the fix at a cause that is not the one acting.

items.sourceSection: A failure taxonomy: classifying what you are looking at

points.v: Ambiguous/underspecified instruction the model filled in — fix the prompt
Confident content not grounded in input or a reliable source — fix via retrieval, tool use, or verification; stronger instructions won't resolve it
Wrong tier for the task, or swapped without re-evaluation — fix via model selection gated on an eval
A recoverable subagent failure looks different from an unrecoverable orchestrator failure — attribution needs a trace spanning both

quiz.q: A support bot states a refund window that appears nowhere in the retrieved policy document, and states it confidently. The team's proposed fix is a firmer instruction: 'never assert facts absent from the source'.
options: Correct — instruction strength is the right lever for ungrounded confident output.
This is ungrounded content; fix it with retrieval, tool use, or verification, not wording.
This is a model mismatch — upgrading to a stronger tier resolves the invented figure.
This is an orchestrator failure; add a trace spanning orchestrator and subagents.
quiz.why: Hallucination is fixed by grounding — retrieval, tool use, or verification. Stronger instructions address prompt failure, a different class in the taxonomy, so they won't resolve it.

items.sourceSection: Discernment: judging the output

points.v: Discernment — one of the four AI Fluency competencies — is judging the quality of what the model produced rather than accepting it at face value
Classify each output as acceptable, needs revision, or needs override, and feed that judgment back into evals and monitoring

quiz.q: A reviewer approves model output whenever it reads well, and no record of those approvals ever reaches the eval suite or the monitoring dashboards. What is missing operationally?
options: A second reviewer to break ties on the borderline outputs.
A model-reported confidence score attached to each generated output.
A stricter written style guide so that 'reads well' becomes an objective, testable standard.
Classify each output acceptable, needs revision, or needs override, feeding that back into evals.
quiz.why: Discernment means judging output quality rather than accepting it at face value; in production the three-way classification must feed evals and monitoring. A second reviewer changes nothing.

items.sourceSection: Connecting observability data to business value

points.v: The observability stack needs a translation layer connecting technical metrics to the business metrics stakeholders track, built at design time rather than after the first business review
Maps to first-contact resolution rate
Maps to average handle time

quiz.q: Six months in, the first business review stalls: the team presents task success rate and p95 latency, and the contact-centre director cannot connect either number to anything she is measured on.
options: Present the same numbers again with a fuller explanation, since the metrics are self-evident once described.
Business metrics are the client's responsibility, not something the observability stack owns.
A translation layer was needed at design time: success rate to first-contact resolution, latency to handle time.
Replace the technical metrics with business metrics entirely and stop tracking latency.
quiz.why: The observability stack needs a business-metric translation layer built at design time, not after the first business review; explaining raw technical metrics never creates the mapping.

items.sourceSection: The 50-session winner that wasn't
items.lead: Any one of three flaws independently invalidates a prompt comparison

points.v: A few points of difference on a high-variance metric needs a sample in the hundreds per group to reach significance
Input distribution not controlled between groups
Choosing the metric after seeing which one moved turns a test into confirmation, not evidence

quiz.q: A team declares a winner: 40 requests per arm, the two groups drawn from different weeks of traffic, and the reported metric picked after seeing which of six measurements moved.
options: Credible — the effect showed up on real traffic, which outweighs sample-size concerns.
Sample far too small, input distribution uncontrolled, and the metric chosen after the fact.
Only the sample size is a real problem; rerun the same design at higher volume.
Only the post-hoc metric choice matters here; the remaining two are standard practice.
quiz.why: All three flaws are present: a high-variance metric needs hundreds per group, input distribution must be controlled, and picking the metric afterwards makes it confirmation, not evidence.

items.sourceSection: Five takeaways
items.lead: Every feasibility verdict takes exactly one of three forms

points.v: Feasible as scoped
Document the load-bearing boundary condition
Not feasible

quiz.q: After an assessment the technical lead writes 'probably doable, we'll see how it goes'. The delivery manager asks for the conclusion stated in the standard form the practice uses.
options: Feasible as scoped; feasible with constraints, documenting the boundary condition; or not feasible.
Green, amber, or red, where amber means further investigation is needed.
Feasible, infeasible, or deferred to a later phase of the engagement.
A confidence percentage between zero and one hundred, accompanied by a short written rationale.
quiz.why: The three verdict forms are feasible as scoped, feasible with constraints, or not feasible. An amber rating hides the load-bearing boundary condition that must be documented.

items.topic: High stakes doesn't force an LLM judge
items.sourceSection: Exercise: define the evaluation framework

points.v: The grading ladder is driven purely by whether a check is deterministic (known value, binary outcome, numeric threshold) or requires interpretation — not by stakes
Cross-claimant data-leakage scan, safety-critical auto-deny check — both stay code-based despite high stakes
Interpretive checks such as summary faithfulness

items.logic: Higher stakes seems to justify a more 'sophisticated' LLM-judge evaluation.

quiz.q: A lending system must never auto-deny an application whose risk score sits below the configured cut-off. A single wrong call here is a reportable regulatory incident. How should that check be graded?
options: LLM-as-judge with a carefully detailed rubric, warranted by the severity of the outcome.
Human review of every decision, since no automated grade is trustworthy at this severity.
A code check comparing the score against the configured cut-off.
An LLM judge calibrated on human labels, escalating its disagreements to a reviewer.
quiz.why: The grading ladder follows determinism, not stakes. A numeric threshold comparison stays code-based; an LLM judge adds interpretation where a binary outcome already exists.

items.sourceSection: Glossary

points.v: 500-599 — server-side failures on an otherwise valid request
Internal Server Error
Service Unavailable
Overloaded Error
Usually transient and resolvable with retry and backoff, distinct from 4xx codes which indicate a client-side problem

quiz.q: During a traffic surge a client's integration logs a burst of 500, 503, and 529 responses. The on-call engineer begins auditing request payloads for malformed fields.
options: The right instinct — these codes signal the requests themselves were malformed.
These are server-side failures on valid requests, usually transient; retry with backoff.
These signal expired authentication; rotating the API key should be the first step.
These signal the rate limit was exceeded; concurrency must be reduced permanently.
quiz.why: The 5xx range covers server-side failures on otherwise valid requests, including 529 Overloaded. Client-side problems are 4xx, so auditing payloads chases the wrong error class.

items.sourceSection: Glossary

points.v: Required under HIPAA between a covered entity or business associate and a vendor handling PHI on its behalf
For Claude deployments, BAA coverage is configuration-specific — the same surface may be covered on one delivery route and not another; check coverage by configuration, not by product

quiz.q: A health system's counsel confirms the paperwork is in place for the vendor's product, and the team plans to move the same workload onto a different delivery route next quarter.
options: Coverage attaches to the product itself, so changing the delivery route needs no further check.
Coverage becomes unnecessary once the data is de-identified at the application layer.
Coverage is granted per customer, so any route that customer uses inherits it.
Coverage is configuration-specific: the same surface may qualify on one route and not another.
quiz.why: BAA coverage for Claude deployments is configuration-specific — check by configuration, not by product. Assuming a product-level answer travels to a new delivery route is the failure.

items.sourceSection: Glossary

points.v: Governs processing of personal data of individuals in the EU/EEA — lawful-basis requirements, data subject rights, controller/processor obligations
Up to 4% of global annual turnover

quiz.q: A European retailer asks what the worst-case financial exposure is if their assistant processes EU customers' personal data with no lawful basis established.
options: Up to four percent of global annual turnover.
A fixed ceiling of twenty million euros, regardless of company size.
Up to four percent of the revenue from the affected product line only.
No fine applies at all while a data processing agreement is in force.
quiz.why: GDPR fines reach up to 4% of global annual turnover, not a share of product revenue; a DPA defines processing terms but never removes the lawful-basis obligation.

items.sourceSection: Glossary

points.v: Data Processing Agreement — contract between a data controller and processor defining how personal data may be handled on the controller's behalf
Covers processing scope, security obligations, sub-processor terms, and breach notification

quiz.q: A client's procurement team asks which contract defines how their customers' personal data may be handled on their behalf, including sub-processor terms and breach notification duties.
options: A business associate agreement covering the vendor's handling obligations.
A service level agreement setting uptime and support commitments.
A data processing agreement between the controller and the processor.
A statement of work listing the deliverables, milestones, and acceptance criteria.
quiz.why: A DPA is the controller-processor contract covering processing scope, security obligations, sub-processor terms, and breach notification; a BAA governs PHI under HIPAA, a different regime.

items.sourceSection: Evals as the gating mechanism for change
items.lead: A multi-turn eval checks three things

points.v: Keeps prior context straight across turns
Answers a follow-up without inventing details never said earlier
Output quality holds as the conversation runs longer
The unit scored is a whole conversation, so it needs its own golden dataset of full transcripts — a single-turn eval set cannot substitute

quiz.q: A chat assistant scores well across a 500-case evaluation set, yet by the sixth exchange it contradicts itself and invents details nobody supplied. What does the evaluation design miss?
options: Add more single-turn cases covering the topics where the contradictions show up.
Enlarge the context window so that earlier turns stop being dropped silently.
Score only each session's final turn, since that is what the user acts on.
Score whole conversations, which needs a golden dataset of full transcripts of its own.
quiz.why: Multi-turn evals check context retention across turns, no invented follow-up details, and quality holding as conversations run long. A single-turn set cannot substitute, however large.

items.sourceSection: The grading ladder: choosing how to grade / Evals as the gating mechanism for change

points.v: Favor volume over perfection — many automatically gradable cases beat a handful of hand-graded ones, since broad cheap coverage catches more regressions and can run on every change
Every model-based eval is an API call, but cost is a secondary constraint — size the dataset against what gives confidence; the bigger risk is under-evaluating

items.logic: Cost discipline suggests trimming to a few high-value hand-curated cases, but one production-breaking change slipping through an undersized suite costs far more than the extra API calls.

quiz.q: A team caps its evaluation set at twenty hand-graded cases, reasoning that every model-graded case is a billable call and that keeping the spend predictable matters more than breadth.
options: Sound cost discipline — a few high-value curated cases beat many cheap ones.
Favor volume of automatically gradable cases; under-evaluating is the bigger risk than spend.
Neither: replace the model-graded cases with manual spot-checks to remove the cost entirely.
Sound, as long as the twenty curated cases are refreshed at every quarter's end.
quiz.why: Eval sets are sized against the confidence they give, favoring broad automatically gradable coverage; one production-breaking regression slipping through costs far more than the API calls.

items.sourceSection: The eval suite that measured the wrong thing
items.lead: An eval suite that exists can still fail in exactly two ways

points.v: Built from a handful of development samples rather than the production input distribution
The golden dataset still holds the old prompt's expected outputs, so it keeps passing
Manual spot-checks are not a substitute — they confirm one input produces one output but say nothing about unknown inputs

quiz.q: A suite built from eight development samples still passes green after a full prompt rewrite, and the team supplements it with a weekly manual look at one production output.
options: Not representative of production inputs, and the expected outputs still encode the old prompt.
Adequate — a green suite plus human spot-checks covers automated and judgment failures.
The only gap is frequency; run the manual spot-check daily rather than weekly.
The suite is fine; the prompt rewrite should have been reverted instead of shipped.
quiz.why: A misconfigured eval suite is unrepresentative and stale, still passing against the old prompt's golden outputs. Spot-checks confirm one output and say nothing about unknown inputs.

items.sourceSection: How to size a use case — Step 3: Project the monthly cost

points.v: Input and output tokens are priced at different rates on all model tiers
(call volume x input tokens x input rate) + (call volume x output tokens x output rate)
Where prompt caching applies, cached input tokens are priced at the cache read rate rather than the standard input rate

quiz.q: A cost model multiplies total monthly tokens by one per-token figure, then applies a flat percentage discount to the share of tokens served from a reused prefix.
options: Correct, provided the single figure is the average of the two published rates.
Only output tokens are billed, so the input volume can safely be ignored.
Input and output price differently and must be computed separately, reused input at the cache read rate.
Token pricing is uniform within a given model tier, so a single blended figure is already exact.
quiz.why: Input and output tokens carry different rates on every tier, so monthly cost sums the two products separately. One blended average misprices any output-heavy workload.

items.sourceSection: Business value and ROI mapping — Complexity note

points.v: Of the four AI properties, working memory (context window) is the most overlooked in feasibility assessments — it rarely shows up during development on small clean inputs but surfaces in production
Skipping any of the four risks missing a constraint that changes the design

quiz.q: A document assistant passed every check on the curated test files and failed in the client's first week on real submissions. Assessments like this most often overlook which capability limit?
options: Output quality in the cases where a user's prompt turns out ambiguous or badly underspecified.
Working memory — the context window, which rarely bites on small clean development inputs.
Instruction following in the presence of a very long system prompt.
Tool-calling reliability once concurrent production load arrives.
quiz.why: Working memory (the context window) is the most overlooked of the four AI properties in feasibility assessments — invisible on small clean dev inputs, decisive on production submissions.

items.sourceSection: Enterprise integration patterns: identity, auth, data, and observability
items.lead: Five layers, each an Architect-owned decision, not an implementation detail

points.v: Comes first and eliminates routes
Least-privilege tool configuration
Identity and authorization
Data handling
Observability
Layers 2-5 operate only within whatever options survive the compliance/entry-point filter

quiz.q: A team specified the auth model, the tool permissions, the redaction rules and the logging plan, then learned that the client's regulator rules out the delivery route the whole design assumed.
options: Unlucky sequencing, but those four completed designs transfer to any route unchanged.
Observability should have come first, since a trustworthy audit trail gates approval for everything else.
Identity and authorization is the foundational layer and was correctly designed first.
Compliance and entry point comes first and eliminates routes; the rest work within survivors.
quiz.why: Of the five integration layers, compliance/entry point is first because it eliminates routes; least-privilege tooling, identity, data handling, and observability operate only within what survives.

items.sourceSection: Security and compliance constraints at the integration layer / Glossary

points.v: Configuration used for geographic pinning of model execution
Geo-pinning is implemented at the delivery route level on CSP-mediated integrations
The pin must be set at the integration layer and verified at request time — it cannot be assumed from the entry point choice

quiz.q: A German client requires that model execution stay physically inside the EU. The team selects an EU-region entry point and records the requirement as satisfied.
options: Pinning is set at the integration layer and must be verified at request time.
Correct — selecting the regional entry point pins where execution happens.
Pinning execution is impossible; only the storage location of data can be controlled.
Declare the region in the system prompt so every request states where it must run.
quiz.why: Geo-pinning via inference_geo is configured at the integration layer on the delivery route and verified per request; it cannot be assumed from the entry-point choice.

items.sourceSection: Security and compliance constraints at the integration layer
items.lead: Work the constraints in this order before any integration design begins

points.v: Identify the governing regulation or policy
Determine which entry point and route are still available
Choose the integration pattern that fits
Document the identity, data handling, and observability requirements that follow
Skipping a step risks building something that works technically but fails legal or security review

quiz.q: An architect picks the integration pattern on day one from a reference architecture, then documents identity and retention decisions around it. Legal review later invalidates the whole choice.
options: Identify the governing regulation, find the surviving entry point and route, then pick the pattern.
Choose the integration pattern first, then map the governing regulation onto whatever pattern was chosen.
Document identity and retention first, since those constrain everything downstream of them.
The order is immaterial provided all four artifacts exist before build begins.
quiz.why: The pre-integration workflow is ordered: regulation, then available entry point and route, then pattern, then identity, data-handling and observability requirements. Skipping ahead fails legal review.

items.sourceSection: Security and compliance constraints at the integration layer

points.v: Privilege preservation (e.g. attorney-client privilege) depends on contractual terms, retention settings, and internal policies
The integration chart only helps mitigate privilege-waiver concerns — it does not establish privilege
The course's compliance material is not legal guidance

items.logic: A compliance/entry-point table reads as declaring a surface 'privileged' or 'compliant', when coverage is set by contract, retention settings, and configuration — so the same surface can qualify on one route and not another.

quiz.q: A law firm points at the vendor's compliance chart and concludes that routing matter documents through the listed surface keeps those documents protected from disclosure.
options: Correct — the chart establishes that the listed surface is a protected one.
Correct, provided the firm also disables request logging inside its own application layer first.
Protection applies automatically to legal-sector customers under the standard terms.
It depends on contract, retention settings, and policy; the chart only mitigates waiver concerns.
quiz.why: Privilege preservation rests on contractual terms, retention settings, and internal policy. The integration chart helps mitigate waiver concerns but never establishes privilege.

items.sourceSection: Place on the experiment-design plane

points.v: How large a difference you expect
How certain you must be before acting
Placement on these two axes determines the right experimental posture, which in turn determines the minimum sample size

quiz.q: A team asks how many runs their new-prompt comparison needs before the result is actionable. What determines the minimum?
options: Sample size is fixed by professional convention at thirty per arm, whatever the question asks.
Expected effect size and confidence requirement place the experiment and set the minimum sample.
Run the comparison until the p-value falls below 0.05, then stop immediately.
Sample size depends only on how much daily traffic is available to split.
quiz.why: The experiment-design plane's axes are expected effect size and confidence requirement; placement determines posture and minimum sample, so a fixed per-arm convention ignores both.

items.sourceSection: What the model's training enforces versus what you own

points.v: The constitution defines the values and behavior Claude should exhibit; latest referenced version January 2026
Used during training to generate learning examples and rank candidate responses
Highest priority in a conflict
Second priority
Complies with Anthropic's guidelines
To operators and users; lowest priority

quiz.q: In a design review, someone asks what happens inside the model when an operator's instruction to be maximally helpful pulls against avoiding a serious harm. Which resolution reflects how Claude's trained values are ordered?
options: Operator instructions win; the operator configured the deployment and accepts the risk.
Being genuinely helpful ranks above ethical behavior, so the user gets an answer.
Being broadly safe carries the highest priority; genuine helpfulness ranks lowest of the four.
The four goals carry equal weight, so the model follows whichever the prompt emphasizes.
quiz.why: The constitution ranks broadly safe, then ethical, then guideline-compliant, then genuinely helpful. An operator instruction cannot promote helpfulness above safety.

items.sourceSection: What the model's training enforces versus what you own

points.v: Priority order (broadly safe > ethical > guideline-compliant > genuinely helpful) is holistic, not strict
Higher-priority goals generally take precedence in a conflict, but the model weighs them together rather than applying a rigid sequence

quiz.q: An engineer builds a decision table asserting the model resolves every value conflict by checking its ranked goals strictly in sequence and stopping at the first one that applies. Is that accurate?
options: No, the ordering is holistic; the goals are weighed together rather than applied as a rigid sequence.
Yes, the ranking is a strict lexicographic sequence evaluated top to bottom.
Yes, but only when the top-ranked goal is not implicated; otherwise ordering is ignored.
No, the goals carry no ranking at all, so no precedence exists between them.
quiz.why: The constitution's priority order is holistic, not strict: higher-priority goals generally take precedence, but the model weighs them together instead of applying a rigid sequence.

items.sourceSection: A layered view: each layer has a job and a blind spot
items.lead: Four layers from Claude outward, each with an owner and a blind spot

points.v: Blocks broad classes of harmful output on every request; blind to your domain policy, data rules, authorization model
Sets role, tone, stated constraints; blind to adversarial/unusual input that talks Claude out of them — not enforcement
Detects disallowed content; blind to actions with side effects and novel attacks a classifier misses
Checks whether this caller may perform this action in this context; blind to content quality and fairness

quiz.q: A team's carefully worded role and constraint text holds up in normal use, but an unusual, persistent user phrasing talks the assistant out of it. Whose blind spot is this?
options: The trained-behavior layer's, owned by Anthropic; its refusal training regressed.
The tool-authorization layer's, owned by the architect; the permissions were too broad.
The screening layer's, owned by Anthropic; the classifier missed a novel attack.
The system-instructions layer's, owned by the architect; stated constraints are not enforcement.
quiz.why: In the four-layer safety stack, system instructions are architect-owned and blind to adversarial input; they state constraints rather than enforce them.

items.sourceSection: Risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems

points.v: User input overrides system instructions
Malicious instructions arrive via retrieved content or tool outputs treated as trusted; user-vector input screening never sees these
Oversized or padded input consumes context or output budget, truncating work or inflating cost
Model is induced to call a side-effecting tool outside policy
Sensitive fields enter the context window or logs where they should not

quiz.q: A retrieval-backed assistant screens every user message before it reaches the model, yet it recently obeyed instructions nobody typed, embedded in a wiki page it pulled in. Which risk category is this?
options: Direct prompt injection: the user's input overrode the system instructions.
Indirect prompt injection: instructions arrived through retrieved content, which user-vector screening never inspects.
Tool and action abuse: the model was induced to call a side-effecting tool.
Token-budget exhaustion: padded retrieved content crowded the system instructions out of context.
quiz.why: Indirect prompt injection arrives via retrieved content or tool outputs treated as trusted; screening the user vector never sees these.

items.sourceSection: A second injection vector: instructions arriving through retrieved content and tool outputs

points.v: "refusal" — returned when a streaming classifier intervenes
Object (since Claude Opus 4.7) with a policy category plus a readable explanation; both null if no named category
cyber, bio, frontier_llm, reasoning_extraction
Tolerate an absent stop_details on models that don't return it; fall back to generic handling

quiz.q: A production handler reads the policy category off blocked-completion metadata. It crashes on some blocked responses but not others, depending on which model served the request. What is the correct handler behavior?
options: Tolerate an absent stop_details and fall back to generic handling on models that do not return it.
Retry the same request until a response carrying stop_details comes back.
Treat a missing stop_details as the cyber policy category, the documented default.
Require stop_details by pinning only models that emit it, so no fallback path is needed.
quiz.why: stop_details is null when no category is named, so handlers must tolerate its absence; treating a missing category as cyber invents a policy verdict.

items.sourceSection: A second injection vector: instructions arriving through retrieved content and tool outputs

points.v: After stop_reason: "refusal", reset the conversation context before continuing — remove or rephrase the triggering turn, or clear the history
Sending the next request on the same refused context returns further refusals

quiz.q: After one request is blocked mid-stream, an assistant keeps returning blocked responses for every follow-up in that session, including harmless ones. What should the application do?
options: Retry the same conversation at a higher temperature to escape the pattern.
Switch to a larger model tier, which blocks less often on borderline turns.
Append a system-prompt note asserting the user is authorized, then resend the history.
Reset the conversation context: remove or rephrase the triggering turn, or clear the history.
quiz.why: After stop_reason "refusal" the context must be reset; sending the next request on the same refused context returns further refusals.

items.sourceSection: Fail open versus fail closed: how your guardrail layer behaves under failure

points.v: Fail-open vs fail-closed is the Architect's choice only for operator-built guardrails (components your team builds, hosts, and configures)
Anthropic's built-in model safety controls are not operator-configurable and do not fail open

quiz.q: In a resilience review, a team proposes a documented degraded mode in which every safety control in the stack, the model provider's own included, passes traffic through when overloaded. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, as long as the degraded mode is an explicit, documented choice.
The provider's built-in safety controls are not operator-configurable and do not fail open; only operator-built guardrails are the architect's choice.
The provider's built-in controls already fail open by default, making the document redundant.
Operator-built guardrails cannot be configured either; failure behavior is fixed by the API.
quiz.why: Fail-open versus fail-closed is the architect's choice only for operator-built guardrails; Anthropic's built-in model safety controls are neither operator-configurable nor fail-open.

items.sourceSection: Skill supply-chain security
items.lead: Audit a skill bundle for two things before trusting it

points.v: Network requests, shell execution, file-system access, credential reads
Operations that don't match the skill's stated job
One of three recorded verdicts every audit ends in
One of three recorded verdicts every audit ends in
Strip the call, sandbox the operation, pin a safer version, then re-audit
An audit misses code fetched at runtime — also run skills sandboxed with least privilege
Source only from a vetted internal registry, verified publishers, and signed releases; never assume the platform vets skills for you

quiz.q: A platform team reads every file in a reusable instructions-plus-scripts bundle, finds no network calls, shell execution, or credential reads, and approves it for production. What still exposes them?
options: Nothing further; a clean read of the bundle is the accepted approval standard.
Only the publisher's signature is missing; a signed release would make the review conclusive.
An audit cannot see code fetched at runtime, so the bundle must also run sandboxed with least privilege.
The audit must re-run on every invocation, since bundle contents change per request.
quiz.why: A skill supply-chain audit misses code fetched at runtime, so static review must be paired with sandboxed execution under least privilege.

items.sourceSection: Where unequal outcomes enter, and what the system must explain

points.v: Unequal outcomes enter a Claude system at four points: the retrieval corpus, the framing of the prompt, the examples used in few-shot prompting, and downstream routing of the output

quiz.q: A lending assistant approves comparable applicants at noticeably different rates. The team wants to know where in their own system unequal outcomes can enter. Where should they look?
options: The model weights, the training corpus, the tokenizer, and the sampling temperature.
The system prompt only; every other component is deterministic code.
The retrieval corpus and the temperature setting; prompt text is neutral by construction.
The retrieval corpus, the prompt's framing, the few-shot examples, and downstream routing of the output.
quiz.why: The four fairness injection points are retrieval corpus, prompt framing, few-shot examples, and downstream routing; model weights and temperature are not deployer-controlled injection points.

items.sourceSection: Where unequal outcomes enter, and what the system must explain

points.v: To replay and explain a single decision, logging must capture: the inputs that drove it, the retrieved context, the model output, and the routing it went through

quiz.q: A regulator asks a deployed system to reconstruct one specific decision made six months ago and explain how it was reached. Which record makes that possible?
options: The inputs that drove it, the retrieved context, the model output, and the routing it went through.
The prompt template version, the model identifier, the latency, and the token counts.
The model output plus the reviewer's approve-or-reject verdict on that item.
An aggregate fairness report covering the cohort that decision belonged to.
quiz.why: Replaying and explaining one decision requires logging its inputs, retrieved context, model output, and routing; request metadata and aggregates cannot reconstruct it.

items.sourceSection: Discernment: judging outputs for unequal treatment

points.v: Discernment (one of the four AI Fluency competencies) is evaluating AI outputs and behaviors — judging whether an output is acceptable, needs revision, or needs override
Applied to fairness: lets a reviewer recognize a skewed or unjustified outcome instead of only confirming a value was produced

quiz.q: Reviewers on a claims queue confirm each output is well-formed and contains a value, then sign off. Skewed outcomes still ship. What capability is the review missing?
options: Faster throughput, so a larger share of the queue gets a second reading.
Judging whether each output is acceptable, needs revision, or needs override, rather than confirming a value was produced.
Access to the model's confidence score for each item, to prioritize what to read.
A stricter output schema, so malformed responses are rejected before review.
quiz.why: Discernment, an AI Fluency competency, is evaluating outputs and behaviors: acceptable, needs revision, or needs override. Confirming a value exists is not evaluation.

items.sourceSection: Diligence: the competency behind human review

points.v: Diligence (one of the four AI Fluency competencies) is ensuring responsible AI collaboration

Applied to deployment: maintain explicit human accountability checkpoints, recognize when automation pressure erodes oversight, and audit workflows for gaps where AI acts without review as automation scales

quiz.q: As a deployment scales, steps that once carried a named human sign-off quietly stop having one, and nobody notices until an incident. Which practice addresses this?
options: Increasing the sampling rate on post-action audits as volume grows.
Raising the model tier so fewer outputs need oversight in the first place.
Maintaining explicit human accountability checkpoints and auditing workflows for gaps where AI acts without review.
Publishing an updated architecture diagram each quarter so the design stays current.
quiz.why: Diligence means explicit human accountability checkpoints and auditing for gaps as automation scales; a faster audit sampling rate cannot restore a checkpoint that disappeared.

items.sourceSection: Routing decisions to people by stakes, not by volume

points.v: Route a decision to a person when it is low-confidence AND either irreversible or high-cost
Let confident, reversible, low-cost decisions through automatically
Reversibility and cost of a wrong decision set the stakes; confidence only determines how much volume gets routed — when they conflict, weight cost and reversibility over confidence

quiz.q: A team must write the rule deciding which of thousands of daily automated decisions get a person. Which rule should they encode?
options: Route everything below the confidence threshold, regardless of what a wrong decision costs.
Route a fixed percentage of daily volume, sampled uniformly across all decision types.
Route every irreversible decision and no others, since confidence cannot be measured at runtime.
Route when a decision is low-confidence and also either irreversible or high-cost.
quiz.why: The routing rule is low confidence AND (irreversible OR high-cost). Confidence alone only sets how much volume routes; reversibility and cost set the stakes.

items.sourceSection: What the reviewer sees decides whether review is accurate
items.lead: Accurate human review requires giving the reviewer three things

points.v: What drove the decision; without these, the reviewer can't tell whether the output is correct
The decision the model produced
Why the item was flagged; without it, the reviewer can't separate an edge case from routine traffic

quiz.q: Reviewers receive the model's output and the record that produced it, yet still cannot tell an unusual case apart from routine traffic they should wave through. What is missing?
options: The model's numeric confidence score for the item.
A comparison against how similar past items were decided.
Why the item was flagged.
The reviewer's own accuracy statistics from previous shifts.
quiz.why: Accurate review needs inputs, the model's output, and the flag reason; without the flag reason a reviewer cannot separate an edge case from routine traffic.

items.sourceSection: Where the human sits is a tradeoff between safety and speed
items.lead: Once a decision is routed to a person, three placement options exist

points.v: Human reviews before the action executes; safer and slower
Human reviews after the action has already executed
Human reviews a sample of actions

quiz.q: Once a decision has been routed to a person, the architect must choose where that person sits relative to execution. What are the options, and what does the safest cost?
options: Before the action, after it as an audit, or on a sample; reviewing before execution is safest and slowest.
Before the action or after it; sampling is a monitoring technique, not a review placement.
Only before the action; anything later is monitoring rather than human review.
On a sample or after the action; pre-action approval is incompatible with automated pipelines.
quiz.why: The three reviewer placements are pre-action approval, post-action audit, and sampled review; sampled review is a placement, not merely monitoring, and pre-action trades speed for safety.

items.sourceSection: What the reviewer sees decides whether review is accurate

points.v: Consent fatigue: a system asks for approval dozens of times in a row and reviewers start clicking through, approving items without reading or giving the quality of review needed

quiz.q: An agent asks for approval dozens of times in a row. Within a week, operators are clicking approve without reading what they approve. What is this effect called?
options: Alert saturation
Consent fatigue
Rubber-stamp drift
Oversight decay
quiz.why: Consent fatigue: repeated approval prompts drive reviewers to click through, approving items without the quality of review the checkpoint was meant to provide.

items.sourceSection: Turning each compliance obligation into a control with evidence

points.v: Never collapse training-use and retention into one claim
Data may be excluded from model training by default while still being retained or monitored for logging, abuse prevention, legal compliance, or configured audit purposes

quiz.q: A privacy officer is told customer data is excluded from model training by default and concludes nothing is kept anywhere. Where does that conclusion break?
options: It holds; exclusion from training is what "not retained" means in this context.
It breaks only if the customer opted into a data-sharing program.
Training use and retention are separate claims; data can still be retained for logging, abuse prevention, legal compliance, or audit.
It breaks because training exclusion applies only to prompts, never to model outputs.
quiz.why: Training-use and retention must never be collapsed into one claim: data excluded from training may still be retained or monitored for other configured purposes.

items.sourceSection: Glossary

points.v: A Business Associate Agreement (BAA) is a contract under HIPAA permitting a vendor to process protected health data on a covered entity's behalf, defining each party's safeguards and liabilities
Without it, handling that data through the vendor is non-compliant regardless of the technical controls in place

quiz.q: A health system has encryption, regional pinning, field-level redaction, and access logging in place before sending patient records to a vendor, but no signed contract governing that vendor's handling. Are they compliant?
options: Yes; the technical controls satisfy the safeguard requirement on their own.
Yes, provided the vendor holds a current third-party security certification.
No, but the gap is procedural, so processing may continue while the contract is negotiated.
No; without a Business Associate Agreement, handling that data through the vendor is non-compliant regardless of technical controls.
quiz.why: A BAA is the HIPAA contract permitting a vendor to process protected health data; absent it, no set of technical controls makes the handling compliant.

items.sourceSection: Glossary

points.v: low, moderate, high impact — sets the security controls a cloud service must meet for US government workloads of that sensitivity
The workload sets the required level, and the delivery route must be authorized at or above it

quiz.q: A federal program's data is rated at a higher sensitivity than the cloud offering the team wants to route through is authorized for. How is this resolved?
options: The workload sets the required impact level; the delivery route must be authorized at or above it.
The route's authorization sets the ceiling; the workload is reclassified down to match it.
Either side may set the level, provided both are documented in the control register.
Authorization levels are advisory; compensating controls substitute for the missing level.
quiz.why: FedRAMP low, moderate, and high impact levels are set by the workload's sensitivity, and the delivery route must hold an authorization at or above it.

items.sourceSection: Glossary

points.v: Data residency: the requirement that data is processed and stored within a specified geographic region, including copies in logs and caches
It is the control behind many data-sovereignty obligations

quiz.q: Requests from an EU deployment terminate in an approved EU region, but the observability pipeline mirrors request metadata to a US bucket and a US cache warms responses. Does the geographic requirement still hold?
options: Yes; the requirement covers where inference runs, not where telemetry lands.
No; the requirement covers processing and storage inside the region, copies in logs and caches included.
Yes, provided the mirrored copies are encrypted in transit and at rest.
Yes, as long as the copies are deleted within the standard retention window.
quiz.why: Data residency requires processing and storage within the specified region, including copies in logs and caches; it is the control behind data-sovereignty obligations.

items.topic: Trained refusals never cover domain policy
items.sourceSection: When trained refusals are mistaken for a domain policy

points.v: Trained refusals cover broad, general-purpose harm only
A deployment-specific rule (e.g. no cross-business-unit record access) never encoded in a classifier, system prompt, or application control is simply unenforced
A normal-looking, in-domain request for a forbidden record then gets answered

items.logic: Reliable refusal of harmful prompts in testing suggests safety training generalizes to your domain access rules, but it never saw them.

quiz.q: An HR assistant passes an extensive red-team suite on harmful content, then answers a politely phrased, perfectly in-domain request for another department's salary records. What happened?
options: The model's safety alignment regressed between versions and needs re-evaluation.
The red-team suite was too small; broader adversarial coverage would have caught it.
The access rule was never encoded in a classifier, system prompt, or application control, so it was simply unenforced.
The request was phrased politely, and politeness defeats trained refusal behavior.
quiz.why: Trained refusals cover broad, general-purpose harm only; a deployment-specific rule encoded nowhere is unenforced, so a normal-looking in-domain request gets answered.

items.topic: One output filter is not a guarded path
items.sourceSection: When a single output filter looks like a finished design

points.v: An output filter inspects only generated text and runs after a tool call has already executed
A model that calls a refund tool completes the irreversible financial action before screening happens
Side-effecting tool calls need their own authorization gate before execution

items.logic: Output filtering looks like the decisive control because it sits closest to the user and is easiest to point to on a diagram.

quiz.q: A billing agent that can issue refunds has one guardrail: a filter inspecting generated text before it reaches the customer. A prompted user gets a refund that policy forbids. Why did the guardrail not stop it?
options: The classifier was evaded by unusual phrasing; a stricter threshold would have caught it.
The filter ran before generation completed and saw only a partial response.
The refund text never reached the customer, so the filter had nothing to inspect.
The filter inspects generated text after the tool call has already executed; the irreversible action was complete.
quiz.why: An output filter screens text only, and runs post-execution; side-effecting tool calls need their own authorization gate before they execute.

items.sourceSection: Fail open versus fail closed: how your guardrail layer behaves under failure

points.v: Absent an explicit choice, a guardrail that errors under load or becomes unreachable lets requests through unscreened — fail open
An operator-built guardrail that silently passes traffic is worse than no guardrail, giving the illusion of protection
Safety controls must fail closed

items.logic: Reliability instinct says degrade gracefully and keep serving rather than block legitimate users.

quiz.q: During a traffic spike, the screening service a team built starts timing out. An engineer proposes that requests continue to the model whenever the check is unavailable, so legitimate users are not blocked. How should this be decided?
options: Reject it; safety controls must fail closed, and a guardrail that silently passes traffic gives the illusion of protection.
Accept it; degrade gracefully and keep serving, since blocking legitimate users is the larger harm.
Accept it, provided the bypassed requests are re-screened later from the logs.
No decision is needed; an unreachable guardrail blocks traffic by default.
quiz.why: Absent an explicit choice a guardrail fails open. Safety controls must fail closed, because an operator-built guardrail that silently passes traffic is worse than none.

items.sourceSection: When routing everything to review makes review meaningless

points.v: Sending every output to a person with only the output and an approve button collapses into rubber-stamping once volume exceeds reading capacity
High-stakes decisions get the same approval as trivial ones
Two failures stack: volume beyond capacity, and missing context to judge against

items.logic: Routing everything to a human feels like the maximally conservative default that needs no judgment about stakes.

quiz.q: Roughly four thousand generated outputs a day go to a queue where one of three reviewers sees the output and an approve button. Six weeks in, approval rates sit near 100% and a serious error shipped. Diagnose it.
options: One failure: the reviewers are under-trained and need a better rubric.
Two failures stack: volume exceeds reading capacity, and reviewers lack the context to judge against.
One failure: the approval interface offers no reject path, so approve is the only outcome.
No design failure; the error was a model regression the reviewers could not have foreseen.
quiz.why: Routing everything to review collapses into rubber-stamping: volume beyond capacity and missing context stack, and high-stakes decisions get the same approval as trivial ones.

items.sourceSection: Build the review-routing rule

points.v: Confidence is not one of the two deciding controls for routing (reversibility and cost of a wrong answer are)
A confident case still routes to a human if irreversible or high-cost
Confidence estimates only how likely the output is wrong, not what happens if it is

items.logic: The natural design is 'low confidence to a human, high confidence through', treating confidence as the primary routing signal.

quiz.q: An architect proposes routing every below-threshold output to a person and letting everything above it through, calling confidence the primary routing signal. What does this miss?
options: Nothing, provided the threshold is calibrated against human-labeled examples.
Only that the threshold should be recalculated separately per decision type.
That high-confidence outputs turn out to be wrong more often than low-confidence ones.
Confidence estimates how likely an output is wrong, not what happens if it is; irreversible or high-cost cases still need a person.
quiz.why: Reversibility and cost of a wrong answer are the two deciding controls for review routing; confidence only determines how much volume gets routed.

items.sourceSection: What the reviewer sees decides whether review is accurate

points.v: Anthropic's agent-autonomy research found requiring sign-off on every action adds friction without meaningful safety gain
The better pattern is monitoring with intervention, concentrating review at higher-value checkpoints such as plan review or exception handling
This is the reasoning behind plan-level review in Claude Code, where a person approves the plan rather than each step

items.logic: Approving every single agent action seems maximally cautious, but it induces consent fatigue and lowers real oversight.

quiz.q: For a high-autonomy deployment agent, a security lead mandates that a human approve each individual command it runs, on the grounds that maximal caution is safest. Is that the strongest oversight design?
options: Yes; per-action sign-off is the maximally cautious design and yields the most oversight.
Yes, provided each approval prompt shows the full command and its arguments.
No; monitoring with intervention, concentrating review at plan review and exception handling, gives more real oversight.
