No; oversight should move entirely to post-action audit of the run logs instead.
quiz.why: Anthropic's agent-autonomy research found per-action sign-off adds friction without meaningful safety gain and induces consent fatigue; plan-level checkpoints are the better pattern.

items.topic: Vendor bias evals don't cover your fairness
items.sourceSection: When fairness is treated as the model provider's problem

points.v: Skew enters at injection points only the deploying architect controls — the retrieval corpus, prompt framing, few-shot examples, downstream routing
A model provider's published fairness evaluations never touched these injection points
Without your own logging you cannot prove where the skew came from when a regulator asks

items.logic: Fairness feels handled upstream because the provider trained the model and published bias-evaluation results.

quiz.q: Asked how their loan-triage deployment guards against unequal treatment, a team cites the model provider's published bias evaluations and considers the question answered. Why is that insufficient?
options: Skew enters at injection points only the deployer controls, and without your own logging you cannot prove where it came from.
The provider's evaluations are valid but expire, so they must be re-requested each quarter.
Provider evaluations cover only English-language inputs, leaving other locales untested.
They are sufficient as long as the deployment uses the model unmodified with no fine-tuning.
quiz.why: Published provider fairness evaluations never touched the retrieval corpus, prompt framing, few-shot examples, or downstream routing, the architect-controlled points where skew enters.

items.sourceSection: When passing entry point selection feels like finishing compliance

points.v: A compliant delivery route (e.g. residency pinned to an approved region) is only a prerequisite
With no named owner and no living evidence artifact, a configuration change can silently break it — such as logging that starts writing request metadata to a second region
The gap surfaces only at audit, when a design document is not a data-flow record

items.logic: Passing the constraint pre-filter produces a visible 'design can move forward' result that feels like compliance is finished.

quiz.q: A design passes the constraint pre-filter, with the delivery route approved and pinned to a permitted region, and the team marks the regulatory workstream done. What have they actually finished?
options: The workstream; an approved, pinned route is what the regulation requires.
Only a prerequisite; without a named owner and a living evidence artifact, a later configuration change silently breaks it.
The technical half; the remaining work is a design document describing the data flow.
Nothing yet; route approval stays provisional until the first audit confirms it.
quiz.why: A compliant delivery route is a prerequisite, not compliance. The gap surfaces only at audit, where a design document is not a data-flow record.

items.sourceSection: What the model's training enforces versus what you own

points.v: Safe behavior baked in before deployment — general by design; never saw your domain policy, data-handling rules, or authorization model
Runtime guardrails you configure per request: system instructions, input/output checks, tool permissions, human review gates; only layer enforcing deployment-specific rules
System instructions shape behavior but enforce policy only when paired with screening, authorization, and review

quiz.q: A team documents its data-handling policy as a paragraph in the system prompt and lists it in the design as an enforced control. A reviewer objects. On what grounds?
options: The paragraph should be shortened, because long constraint text degrades instruction following.
Policy text belongs in the operator's contract, never in a runtime prompt.
System instructions shape behavior but enforce policy only when paired with screening, authorization, and human review.
Training-time alignment already covers data handling, which makes the paragraph redundant.
quiz.why: Inference-time control is the only layer enforcing deployment-specific rules, and system instructions alone are not enforcement without screening, authorization, and review.

items.sourceSection: Risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems

points.v: user input, retrieved content, tool outputs, the model's own output, and the logs
Walk the request and data paths together; at each entry point ask what an adversary could do and which control stands in the way
Look for anywhere a plausible attack meets no control

quiz.q: Preparing a threat model, a team plans to walk every place an adversary could influence or observe their Claude system. Their draft lists user input, retrieved content, and tool outputs. What is still missing?
options: The system prompt and the model weights.
The API key and the network transport.
The retrieval index refresh job and the embedding model.
The model's own output, and the logs.
quiz.why: The five vulnerability-assessment entry points are user input, retrieved content, tool outputs, the model own output, and the logs; system prompt and weights are not entry points.

items.sourceSection: Placing screening and authorization so the system degrades safely
items.lead: The two check types fail in opposite ways and are chained in series, never used alone

points.v: Can be evaded by phrasing
Brittle — blocks exactly what it was programmed to detect, misses the unanticipated, over-blocks anything resembling a restricted pattern
No control catches everything, so identify what each misses and cover that gap with a different control

quiz.q: A team replaces a brittle regular-expression blocklist that kept over-blocking with a judge model, and treats the swap as a clean upgrade. What is wrong with the reasoning?
options: A judge model is strictly weaker; deterministic rules should always be preferred for screening.
The two check types fail in opposite ways and belong chained in series; a classifier alone can be evaded by phrasing.
The judge model must be the same model being evaluated, so its verdicts stay consistent.
Nothing is wrong; a calibrated judge model supersedes deterministic rules entirely.
quiz.why: Model-based classifiers can be evaded by phrasing and deterministic rules are brittle; the two are chained in series, never used alone.

items.sourceSection: Where unequal outcomes enter, and what the system must explain
items.lead: Transparency serves three audiences needing different slices of the same record

points.v: The affected person; needs the reason in terms they can act on
Ask whether similar cases were treated comparably
Needs the full trace for any flagged decision
Who asks determines what the system explains

quiz.q: One decision record is requested by the applicant it affected, by a supervisory authority, and by the engineers debugging the flag. Should the system return the same explanation to each?
options: No; the affected person needs a reason they can act on, the authority whether similar cases were treated comparably, the team the full trace.
Yes; one complete trace serves all three, and anything less risks inconsistency between accounts.
Yes for the authority and the engineers; the affected person receives no explanation.
No; each audience needs a separately generated record, logged independently at decision time.
quiz.why: Transparency serves three audiences, users, regulators, and the debugging team, needing different slices of the same record; who asks determines what the system explains.

items.sourceSection: Glossary

points.v: The compliance control register is a table mapping each obligation to its technical control, an accountable owner, and an evidence artifact
A regulated deployment is audited as a register rather than asserted as a narrative
Because configurations drift and artifacts go stale, it is revalidated on a regular cadence and spans security, legal, and platform owners who must agree on who holds what

quiz.q: At audit, a regulated team presents a well-written narrative describing how each obligation is met. The auditor asks for something else instead. What?
options: A signed attestation from the model provider covering each obligation.
The full request logs for the audit period, sampled at random.
An architecture diagram annotated with the regulated data flows.
A table mapping each obligation to its technical control, an accountable owner, and an evidence artifact.
quiz.why: A regulated deployment is audited as a compliance control register, not asserted as a narrative, and the register is revalidated on cadence because configurations drift.

items.sourceSection: Glossary

points.v: HIPAA drives a specific delivery requirement: deliver through a HIPAA-ready plan or first-party API under a signed BAA

quiz.q: A hospital's triage assistant will process patient records. The team's default is whichever cloud marketplace their procurement already covers. What constrains that choice?
options: Any route works once the records are encrypted at rest and in transit before transmission.
Any route authorized at FedRAMP moderate or above satisfies the requirement.
Delivery must go through a HIPAA-ready plan, or the first-party API under a signed BAA.
Only a self-hosted deployment satisfies it; all managed delivery routes are excluded.
quiz.why: HIPAA drives a specific delivery requirement, a HIPAA-ready plan or first-party API under a signed BAA; procurement convenience does not override it.

items.sourceSection: Placing screening and authorization so the system degrades safely

points.v: Input filters and prompt screening watch the conversation, but a skill's malicious logic was baked into the bundle upstream and never appears there
Output monitoring may catch a downstream effect only after the code has already run
The defense must move earlier: pre-use audit of the bundle plus runtime confinement

items.logic: A guarded path that screens inputs and outputs seems to cover anything a skill does, but the skill's code never enters the screened conversation.

quiz.q: A team argues their guarded path is complete: every user message is filtered on the way in and every response monitored on the way out, so any packaged automation they install is covered. Where is the gap?
options: A bundle's malicious logic never enters the screened conversation; the defense must move earlier, to pre-use audit plus runtime confinement.
The gap is only in input filtering; output monitoring catches bundle behavior in time.
There is no gap, provided the bundle's outputs pass through the same monitor.
The gap closes by raising the classifier's sensitivity on bundle-generated content.
quiz.why: Input and output screening watch the conversation, but a skill's code was baked into the bundle upstream; output monitoring catches effects only after the code runs.

items.sourceSection: Where unequal outcomes enter, and what the system must explain

points.v: Logging for transparency and minimizing data are not in conflict: they need the same log, governed differently
The decision log is itself in scope for the compliance register — under HIPAA or GDPR its logged inputs and retrieved context hold sensitive personal data
Apply minimization, retention limits, and access controls to it, and map it as a named control

items.logic: Capturing inputs, retrieved context, output, and routing on every decision looks like a direct violation of data minimization, forcing a choice between the two.

quiz.q: A privacy lead says capturing inputs, retrieved context, output, and routing on every decision directly violates data minimization, and asks the team to pick one goal or the other. How should the architect respond?
options: Minimization wins; log only the output and a decision identifier, then reconstruct the rest on demand.
They need the same log, governed differently: apply minimization, retention limits, and access controls, and map it as a named control.
Transparency wins; decision logs are exempt from minimization because they exist for regulators.
Keep two logs, a full unrestricted trace for debugging and a redacted one for auditors.
quiz.why: Transparency logging and data minimization are not in conflict; the decision log is itself in scope for the compliance register and governed as a named control.

items.sourceSection: A discovery call is a structured elicitation, not a conversation
items.lead: Discovery is run as a three-step filter

points.v: Hear the business goal in plain language
Convert it into requirements, assumptions, and unresolved constraints
Write those down before the conversation moves on

quiz.q: An architect leaves a 45-minute stakeholder call having understood the business goal perfectly, and plans to write everything up after the next two calls. What did that call fail to do?
options: Listen for the goal, translate it into requirements, assumptions and open constraints, and record them before the conversation moved on.
Obtain a signed scope statement in which the stakeholder's executive sponsor confirms the business goal, the budget envelope, and the delivery date.
Produce a shared architecture diagram the stakeholder could review ahead of the next working session.
Rank the emerging requirements into a prioritised backlog agreed with the product owner.
quiz.why: The discovery three-step filter is listen, translate, record — and recording happens before the conversation moves on, not after two more calls.

items.sourceSection: A discovery call is a structured elicitation, not a conversation
items.lead: Discovery forces a vague stakeholder statement into four buckets

points.v: What the system must do
Stakeholders rarely volunteer this; Architect must ask for it explicitly
What the system must cost
What the system must prove

quiz.q: A stakeholder talks at length about what the new assistant should handle, the budget ceiling it must respect, and the metrics that would prove it worked. What is almost certainly still missing?
options: Nothing material — capability, cost and proof already cover the ground discovery needs.
The delivery timeline; without committed dates the scope of the build cannot be bounded.
The prohibitions: stakeholders rarely volunteer what the system must not do, so ask explicitly.
An inventory of the systems it will integrate with, which matters more than stated goals.
quiz.why: Discovery's four categories are must do, must not do, must cost, must prove; the must-not-do is rarely volunteered and must be asked for explicitly.

items.sourceSection: A discovery call is a structured elicitation, not a conversation
items.lead: Each discovery item becomes one row with four columns

points.v: The stakeholder statement as said
The constraint that statement implies
The architectural decision that constraint forces
Documented when the constraint is not yet confirmed

quiz.q: Your discovery notes are a bulleted list of stakeholder quotes. A reviewer asks which architectural choices each quote forced. How should each line have been captured?
options: As a user story with acceptance criteria, a story-point estimate, a priority, and the delivery sprint it has been assigned to.
As a row: the statement as said, the constraint it implies, the decision it forces, the assumption if unconfirmed.
As a risk entry carrying likelihood, impact, a mitigation, and a named accountable owner.
As the quote annotated with the diagram component it maps onto in the design.
quiz.why: The translation table row holds statement, constraint, decision and assumption; a bare quote records neither what the constraint forced nor what remains unconfirmed.

items.sourceSection: Present a tradeoff so the stakeholder can act on it
items.lead: Present a tradeoff through four questions

points.v: What do we gain
What do we give up
Cost to undo the decision after the system is built around it — most-skipped element, most often changes the meeting
In regulated environments, what this does to our compliance posture

quiz.q: You lay out two architectures with benefits, drawbacks and cost fully explained, and the sponsor picks the cheaper one within minutes. Which unasked question most often changes that meeting?
options: How long each option takes to implement with the team currently available.
What it costs to undo the choice once the system is built around it.
Which vendor behind each option offers the stronger long-term support agreement.
How each option scores against the delivery team's existing skills and tooling.
quiz.why: The tradeoff frame asks gain, give up, reversal cost, compliance posture; reversal cost is the most-skipped element and the one that most often changes the meeting.

items.sourceSection: The feedback loop decides which signals reach a stakeholder
items.lead: Feedback loop sits above observability, runs five sequential steps

points.v: What is the system showing us?
What needs attention now vs. what can wait?
Does this need a team fix, stakeholder review, or no action?
What correction, guardrail update, or escalation is required?
Did the response work, and does the rule need to change?

quiz.q: A retro finds the team saw the signal, went straight to a fix, and never checked whether the fix worked or whether the governing rule needed changing. What sequence should the routine follow?
options: Detect, alert, escalate, remediate, close the incident record.
Monitor, measure, report, optimise, then repeat on the next cycle.
Observe, orient, decide, act, looping continuously as conditions change.
Signals, triage, decide, act, review.
quiz.why: The feedback loop runs signals, triage, decide, act, review; skipping review means nobody confirms the correction worked or updates the rule.

items.sourceSection: The observability stack that replaced the feedback loop

points.v: Collects and displays signals; observability records what happened
Maps each signal to a trigger, an owner, and a required action; determines what to do about it

quiz.q: A CTO asks what your proposed governance work adds on top of the monitoring dashboards they already paid for. Which answer draws the right line?
options: Dashboards collect and display signals; the feedback loop maps each signal to a trigger, an owner, and a required action.
Dashboards show the current state of the system; the feedback loop preserves the history auditors need to reconstruct what happened and when.
Dashboards serve engineers; the feedback loop is that same data reformatted for an executive audience.
Dashboards cover infrastructure health; the feedback loop covers model quality and output metrics.
quiz.why: A dashboard collects and displays; observability records what happened. The feedback loop decides what to do about a signal — trigger, owner, required action.

items.sourceSection: The feedback loop decides which signals reach a stakeholder
items.lead: An SLA is a commitment that makes three things clear

points.v: What are we measuring
What counts as a breach
What happens when a breach occurs

quiz.q: A client contract promises 'high availability and fast responses, continuously monitored.' Legal asks whether that is actually enforceable. What must the commitment make clear?
options: What is measured, what counts as a breach, and what happens when a breach occurs.
The uptime percentage, the latency percentile, and the vendor performing the monitoring.
The escalation contacts, the review cadence, and the format of the monthly report.
The service scope, the covered support hours, and the contract renewal terms.
quiz.why: An SLA makes three things clear: the measure, the breach definition, and the breach consequence. 'Continuously monitored' supplies none of them.

items.sourceSection: Glossary
items.lead: Governance table maps each production signal to three things

points.v: What triggers a review for that signal
The Architect's response to that signal
Any regulatory checkpoint tied to that signal
Must exist before launch; the mechanism that turns policy into an operating routine

quiz.q: A regulated deployment goes live with an approved AI policy and a signed risk assessment. Weeks later nobody can say what should have prompted a review of anything. What was never built?
options: A standing quarterly steering committee bringing the compliance, product and engineering leads around one table with a published agenda.
An expanded set of alert thresholds, tuned after observing real production traffic.
A per-signal table of review triggers, Architect responses, and regulatory checkpoints, in place before launch.
A RACI matrix assigning ownership of each policy clause across the delivery team.
quiz.why: The governance table maps each production signal to a review trigger, an Architect response and a regulatory checkpoint; it turns policy into an operating routine before launch.

items.sourceSection: Documentation that survives your absence
items.lead: Architecture documentation must serve three readers

points.v: Had no part in the build
Needs evidence a specific control is live
Returns to the system months later
A document built for one reader and not the others is incomplete even when detailed

quiz.q: A 40-page architecture pack is praised by the incoming engineering team as the clearest handover they have seen. The compliance reviewer cannot use any of it. How should the pack be judged?
options: Incomplete — it must equally serve the auditor and the Architect returning months later.
Acceptable — depth for the team inheriting the build is the primary handover goal.
Acceptable — compliance evidence belongs in a separate control repository, not the architecture pack.
Incomplete — it should be condensed until every audience can read the same summary.
quiz.why: Architecture documentation serves three readers: inheriting engineer, auditor, returning Architect. Built for one and not the others, it is incomplete however detailed.

items.sourceSection: Documentation that survives your absence
items.lead: For a compliance reviewer, documentation carries four fields per control

points.v: Each regulatory obligation
The technical control that satisfies it
That control's owner
Concrete proof the control is operating: signed agreement, configuration screen, authorization record, returned log query
A control asserted with no artifact is a claim, not proof

quiz.q: A register lists every regulatory obligation, the technical control that satisfies it, and a named owner for each. The external reviewer rejects it anyway. What is missing?
options: A residual-risk rating for each obligation, calculated after the control is applied.
A cross-reference from each obligation to the specific clause of the regulation it derives from, plus the date it was last reviewed.
Sign-off from each owner's line manager confirming the control was actually implemented.
Concrete proof each control operates: signed agreement, configuration screen, authorization record, returned log query.
quiz.why: The control register's fourth field is the evidence artifact; a control asserted without one is a claim, not proof, however well owned.

items.sourceSection: Glossary
items.lead: Records which Claude entry point owns which task and why

points.v: Direct API, Claude Code, Bedrock, Vertex, Microsoft Foundry
Written before integration begins
Prevents an entry point chosen for one task from quietly taking on another because routing was never documented

quiz.q: Eighteen months on, a route stood up for one batch job now serves three unrelated workloads and nobody recalls deciding that. Which artifact, written earlier, would have prevented the drift?
options: A per-workload rate-limit policy enforced centrally at the API gateway.
A record of which Claude entry point owns which task and why, written before integration begins.
An architecture diagram showing every service that currently calls the model.
A cost-allocation tagging scheme that separates each workload's spend cleanly.
quiz.why: The entry-point-responsibility map records which entry point owns which task and why; without it, routing was never documented and an entry point quietly absorbs other work.

items.sourceSection: Entry point selection returns with the full production picture

points.v: Model identifier strings differ across routes
Feature availability on a CSP-mediated route can lag the direct API
Each is an integration point with its own authentication, logging, and failure-mode profile

quiz.q: A team wants to run one workload against the direct API and a cloud provider's managed route, treating the second as a drop-in failover. What do you warn them about?
options: Failover is safe once both routes are pinned to the same model version string, the same temperature, and the same system prompt.
The real risk is latency variance; behaviour is identical because the weights are identical.
Identifier strings differ, managed-route features can lag the direct API, and auth, logging and failure modes differ.
Nothing structural — a managed cloud route is the direct API with billing attached.
quiz.why: Each entry-point boundary is a distinct integration point: model identifier strings differ, CSP-mediated feature availability can lag, and authentication, logging and failure profiles are its own.

items.lead: A customer outcome document covers six fields

points.v: The use case and its scope boundary
The metric before deployment
The metric after deployment
The control that makes the result auditable
Responsible for ongoing measurement
Potential to reuse the pattern for other engagements
The before-and-after outcome plus the reuse notes are what make it reusable IP rather than a technical record

quiz.q: A closing deliverable records the use case and its scope, the measured before-and-after, and the control making the result auditable. A partner lead says it is still just a technical record. What is missing?
options: A cost breakdown showing the deployment's return on investment for the customer.
A sanitised version cleared by the customer for use as a public reference.
A funded backlog of the enhancements the customer agreed to build next.
A named owner for ongoing measurement, and notes on reusing the pattern elsewhere.
quiz.why: The customer outcome document's six fields end with the measurement owner and reuse potential; the before-and-after plus reuse notes are what make it reusable IP.

items.sourceSection: Orientation: what you will be able to do by the end
items.lead: Deployment lifecycle runs five phases in sequence

points.v: Discovery → design → handoff → monitoring → iteration
Documentation
The feedback loop
Entry-point selection together with the outcome document

quiz.q: A new architect asks how the stages of an engagement line up with the artifacts she is expected to produce. Which mapping is right?
options: Discovery, pilot, rollout, support, renewal; support is documentation and renewal is the feedback loop.
Design, build, test, deploy, operate; deploy is documentation and operate is the feedback loop.
Discovery, design, monitoring, handoff, iteration; monitoring precedes handoff so alerting already exists on the day the system goes live.
Discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration; handoff is documentation, monitoring and iteration the feedback loop.
quiz.why: The deployment lifecycle runs discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration in that order; handoff is documentation, and monitoring plus iteration are the feedback loop.

items.sourceSection: The discovery call that turned into a design session

points.v: A discovery call must finish the four-category question set (must do / must not do / must cost / must prove) before any architecture is proposed
Sketching a plausible solution partway through the call is the named failure mode, however productive it feels

items.logic: Confirming a mid-call sketch feels like alignment, but it stops the questioning, so hidden constraints (a human-authorization gate, PHI handling, multi-jurisdiction residency) surface only weeks later in compliance review.

quiz.q: Twenty minutes into a first call you sketch an architecture on the whiteboard; the stakeholder says it matches what they pictured, and the rest of the hour refines it. Assess the call.
options: A strong outcome — the stakeholder confirmed alignment on the solution unusually early.
The named failure mode — architecture was proposed before the must do, must not do, must cost, must prove set was finished.
Acceptable — sketching is part of discovery provided the drawing is captured in the notes.
A problem only if the sketch is later treated as a binding commitment, rather than as one option among several still on the table.
quiz.why: Discovery must complete the four-category question set before any architecture is proposed; confirming a mid-call sketch feels like alignment but stops the questioning, so hidden constraints surface in compliance review.

items.topic: Observability stack is not a feedback loop
items.sourceSection: The observability stack that replaced the feedback loop

points.v: A fully live observability stack (dashboards, alerts, data flowing) does not mean stakeholder feedback is covered
Slow quality drift can sit visible in the collected data for weeks and never trigger a review, because no governance rule mapped that signal to a trigger and owner

items.logic: Alerts fire only on thresholds someone defined, so a dashboard collecting a signal nobody owns is exactly as blind as not collecting it.

quiz.q: A production deployment has dashboards, alerting and complete telemetry. An output-quality decline sat in the collected data for a month with nobody reviewing it. What best explains the gap?
options: The telemetry was too coarse; finer-grained quality metrics would have surfaced the decline.
Alert fatigue — the alert fired but was lost among lower-priority notifications.
No governance rule mapped that signal to a trigger and an owner, so no review fired.
The stack was fine; the gap was the stakeholder review meeting's cadence.
quiz.why: An observability stack is not a feedback loop. Alerts fire only on thresholds someone defined, so finer metrics nobody owns stay exactly as blind.

items.sourceSection: Present a tradeoff so the stakeholder can act on it

points.v: "Limit placement" = deciding in advance which one or two limitations a demo will name, and framing them as intentional scope boundaries
Naming them builds buyer confidence, especially in regulated industries (healthcare, financial services, public sector)

items.logic: Naming a weakness feels risky, but a vague or deflected answer drops confidence, while a clearly scoped boundary reads as rigor.

quiz.q: Preparing a demo for a hospital network's buying committee, a colleague argues you should not raise the two areas where the system is weakest unless someone asks. What is the better play?
options: Decide in advance which one or two limits the demo names, framed as intentional scope boundaries.
Leave them out; naming a weakness in front of a buying committee costs you confidence.
Disclose every known limitation exhaustively so nothing can later be called a surprise.
Defer all limitation questions to a written follow-up that legal reviews first.
quiz.why: Limit placement chooses in advance which limits a demo names as scope boundaries; withholding produces the vague or deflected answer that actually drops buyer confidence.

items.sourceSection: Entry point selection returns with the full production picture

points.v: Regional availability on Bedrock and Vertex requires explicit configuration
Defaulting to a global endpoint is the common pattern that breaks a data-residency requirement

items.logic: The provider's default/global endpoint looks like the safe standard choice with residency handled at the account or region level, but on Bedrock/Vertex residency is never automatic.

quiz.q: A German insurer requires all inference to stay in-region. The team deploys on a major cloud provider's managed service using its default endpoint and reports the requirement satisfied. Assess.
options: Satisfied — the provider's default endpoint honours the region configured on the account.
Satisfied once the account is billed to an EU legal entity, all request logs are retained in Europe, and a DPA is signed.
Not satisfied — regional availability needs explicit configuration; a global endpoint is how residency commonly breaks.
Not satisfied — managed cloud routes can never meet a hard data-residency requirement.
quiz.why: On Bedrock and Vertex regional availability requires explicit configuration; residency is never automatic at account level, so the default global endpoint is the common breakage.

items.sourceSection: A discovery call is a structured elicitation, not a conversation
items.lead: Five experience words signal more discovery is needed, not requirements

points.v: Seamless, easy, fast, simple, intuitive
What would break that experience?
What must the user never notice?
What has to happen behind the scenes?
What must still be true when something goes wrong?

quiz.q: The stakeholder's brief is one line: 'it just has to feel seamless.' The PM logs that as the primary requirement. What should happen next?
options: Record it as the primary requirement, then pin down exactly what 'seamless' will mean in the acceptance criteria agreed with the product owner.
Benchmark competitor products to establish what seamless means for this market segment.
Ask the stakeholder to rank seamlessness against cost and the committed delivery date.
Treat it as unfinished discovery: probe what breaks it, what users never notice, what happens behind the scenes, what holds under failure.
quiz.why: Seamless is one of the five experience words; it signals more discovery is needed, so the four probes must convert it before anything is recorded as a requirement.

items.sourceSection: Glossary / A discovery call is a structured elicitation

points.v: Course's reserved term for the core discovery move: converting a stakeholder preference ("seamless", "fast", "simple") into a testable, bounded constraint
Named the most important skill in discovery
A preference only tells you where to investigate; the follow-up questions produce the constraint itself

quiz.q: A junior architect reports a good call: the client wants it 'fast and simple,' and he has logged both as constraints in the requirements sheet. What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing — logging the client's own words verbatim is what best preserves their original intent for the design work that follows.
A preference is not a constraint; it shows where to investigate, and follow-up questions produce the testable bound.
Two constraints is far too few; a first call should surface a dozen or more.
Speed and simplicity conflict, so one of them must be dropped before design begins.
quiz.why: Translation — named the most important skill in discovery — converts a preference into a testable, bounded constraint; transcribing the preference performs none of that work.

items.sourceSection: Glossary

points.v: Captures, for each architectural choice, the decision, the alternatives rejected, and the tradeoff each resolved
A diagram records what the system is, never why
Without the record, a successor reverses a load-bearing choice for an understandable wrong reason

quiz.q: A successor team rips out a queue the original design deliberately introduced, calling it needless latency. The handover pack contained full, accurate diagrams. What was missing from it?
options: A performance baseline recording the latency the queue was expected to add.
A change-control gate requiring the original architect to approve any removal.
Annotated diagrams labelling each component with the function it performs.
For each choice: the decision, the alternatives rejected, and the tradeoff each one resolved.
quiz.why: The design rationale record carries decision, rejected alternatives and resolved tradeoff; a diagram records what the system is, never why, so a successor reverses load-bearing choices.

items.sourceSection: The feedback loop decides which signals reach a stakeholder

points.v: In regulated deployments, some governance rows are schedule-triggered rather than threshold-triggered — e.g. periodic output audits for a documentation obligation, scheduled confirmation an environment still meets residency rules
These are design-time obligations; their rows must be in place before launch

items.logic: Monitoring intuition says a review fires only when a metric crosses a threshold, so a system with nothing going wrong appears to need no review at all.

quiz.q: In a regulated deployment every governance row is wired to a metric threshold. A full year passes, nothing crosses a threshold, and no review is ever held. Is the design sound?
options: Yes — nothing crossed a threshold, so nothing warranted anyone's attention.
Yes, provided the thresholds were retuned against the first quarter's real traffic.
No — some rows must be schedule-triggered: periodic output audits, scheduled residency confirmations.
No — thresholds should be lowered until reviews fire at a predictable rate.
quiz.why: Regulated governance rows can be schedule-triggered rather than threshold-triggered; these are design-time obligations whose rows must exist before launch, even when nothing goes wrong.

items.sourceSection: Configuring Claude tooling and environments for teams
items.lead: Skills reach teams through exactly four distribution mechanisms

points.v: Uploaded at Organization settings > Skills; available org-wide at once
Assigned to a group or org; install prefs (required, installed-by-default, available, not available); version-controlled updates from a connected repository; rollback
.claude/skills/; versioned with the repository; scoped to the projects that carry them
Called programmatically by the partner's own products; explicit version pinning

quiz.q: A platform team wants their code-review helper to live in the repo it serves, update through ordinary pull requests, and never appear for teams that don't check out that repo. Which route fits?
options: Upload it at Organization settings > Skills so every team receives it at once, then ask the others to ignore it.
Bundle it in a plugin assigned to that group, with install preferences and version-controlled updates from the connected repository.
Commit it under .claude/skills/ in the project, versioned with the repository and scoped to the projects that carry it.
Expose it as an API Skill with an explicitly pinned version, called programmatically by the products that need it.
quiz.why: Tests the four Skills distribution mechanisms: project Skills in .claude/skills/ are repo-scoped. The plugin trap also syncs from a repository, but assigns by group, not per checkout.

items.sourceSection: Configuring Claude tooling and environments for teams

points.v: Server-managed settings are a separate settings-delivery channel, not a fifth Skills distribution mechanism
Delivered from Anthropic's servers when users authenticate
Refreshes on an hourly polling cycle

items.logic: It's centrally administered and applies org-wide like the four Skills mechanisms, so it looks like another way to distribute Skills.

quiz.q: An admin wants a single centrally administered channel that arrives when people sign in to carry both org-wide configuration and the team's packaged capabilities, arguing the two are the same kind of thing. What's wrong?
options: Server-managed settings form a separate settings-delivery channel, delivered from Anthropic's servers at authentication; the four Skills distribution mechanisms stay distinct.
Nothing - it is centrally administered and applies org-wide like the others, so it is simply a fifth Skills distribution mechanism.
It applies only at install time, so nothing pushed through it reaches users who authenticated earlier.
It works, but every user must opt in per machine before either configuration or capabilities are delivered to them.
quiz.why: Server-managed settings arrive at authentication and refresh hourly - a settings channel, not a fifth Skills distribution mechanism. Central org-wide administration does not make it one.

items.sourceSection: Configuring Claude tooling and environments for teams
items.lead: The Architect owns four team-setup decisions

points.v: Environment
Rollout
Skills distribution
Spend

quiz.q: A lead reports the team setup is finished: everyone starts from the same baseline, access is staged in waves, and packaged capabilities have an agreed delivery route. What still has no owner?
options: Incident escalation ownership - naming who handles what once an operational issue leaves the team entirely.
Prompt-writing standards, so every member phrases requests to the model in one agreed house style.
Nothing further - baseline, staging and delivery route are the complete set of decisions to settle.
Spend - model defaults, allowlists, effort guidance and caps are the fourth decision the Architect owns.
quiz.why: The Architect's four team-setup decisions are environment, rollout, Skills distribution and spend. The complete-set trap drops spend, leaving cost entirely ungoverned after launch.

items.sourceSection: Configuring Claude tooling and environments for teams
items.lead: Team cost guardrails have four components

points.v: Which model a session starts on
Which models the team may switch to
How hard the model works on a task
Spend, rate, and per-user caps

quiz.q: Monthly cost tripled even though every session starts on the cheap model and only two models can be switched to. The lead insists the budget controls are already fully configured.
options: Correct - with a starting model and a restricted switch list in place, no further budget levers exist to set.
Two levers are unset: how hard the model works on a task, and spend, rate and per-user caps.
The remaining lever is per-repository token quotas declared in the project CLAUDE.md and enforced at session start.
The remaining lever is administrator approval of each individual session before the model is allowed to run.
quiz.why: Cost guardrails have four components: model defaults, allowlists, effort guidance and caps. The trap treats defaults plus allowlists as complete, so effort and caps stay unbounded.

items.sourceSection: Configuring Claude tooling and environments for teams
items.lead: Roll out champion-and-batch, never a single switch-on

points.v: One champion per department/team gets access first, proves the workflow in practice, then adoption seeds batch by batch
200-person org, four departments
One champion per department
Two weeks to convert a real workflow (e.g. code-review assist, test-generation step)
45-minute session for a first batch of five peers

quiz.q: A 200-person org across four departments plans to switch everyone on next Monday behind a single company-wide demo. What should replace that plan?
options: One champion per department first; two weeks to convert a real workflow; then a 45-minute session for five peers.
One champion for the whole org proves the workflow, then all four departments onboard together in a single session.
Grant everyone access Monday, then run a mandatory 45-minute training per department over the following two weeks.
Enable one department completely as a quarter-long pilot, then repeat department by department once its metrics land.
quiz.why: Champion-and-batch rollout: one champion per department, two weeks on a real workflow, then batches of five peers. The single-champion trap seeds nothing in the other three departments.

items.sourceSection: Improving developer workflows with AI tooling
items.lead: Two named adoption failure modes; access alone is not adoption

points.v: Few developers use it heavily, rest barely touch it; team never realizes the gain or standardizes; mitigation: champion-and-batch rollout
Team uses Claude only as a question-answering box, never advances to tool use, repository-aware assistance, or packaged Skills

quiz.q: Six weeks after access was granted, three engineers account for nearly all usage, everyone else has barely opened it, and no shared practice has emerged on the team.
options: The team is using it only as a question-answering box; the fix is advancing to tool use and repository-aware assistance.
Expected - access was provisioned, so adoption follows on its own once the remaining seats finish rolling out.
Seat over-provisioning; cut licences back to the three active engineers and re-evaluate demand for the rest next quarter.
Lumpy adoption: a few use it heavily, the gain is never realized or standardized; mitigate with champion-and-batch rollout.
quiz.why: Lumpy adoption, not stalling at basic chat - the problem is who uses it, not how deeply. The basic-chat trap misreads uneven usage as shallow usage.

items.sourceSection: Improving developer workflows with AI tooling

points.v: Taking responsibility for verifying and vouching for the outputs we use or share

quiz.q: An engineer merges an AI-drafted migration and says that since the model produced it and the pipeline went green, a production incident afterwards would not really be on them.
options: Half right - accountability sits with whoever approved the model defaults and permission posture the team works under.
Whoever uses or shares an output owns verifying it and vouching for it; that responsibility does not transfer.
No - responsibility moved to review the moment a second approver signed off on the migration.
Right - a green pipeline is the agreed gate, so accountability passes to whoever owns that pipeline's checks.
quiz.why: Deployment diligence: you verify and vouch for the outputs you use or share. The green-pipeline trap treats an automated check as a transfer of responsibility.

items.sourceSection: Improving developer workflows with AI tooling
items.lead: Four dimensions gate AI output before it reaches production

points.v: Correctness
Security
Maintainability
Human understanding

quiz.q: Before AI-assisted changes reach production, a lead proposes gating them on latency, cost, test coverage and code style, and asks whether that is the right set of four.
options: No - the four gates are correctness, security, latency, and rollback readiness before anything reaches production.
Yes, provided coverage thresholds are enforced in CI so nothing merges below the agreed percentage.
No - the four dimensions gating output before production are correctness, security, maintainability, and human understanding.
Nearly - keep coverage and style, but replace latency and cost with correctness and security for AI-assisted changes.
quiz.why: The verification checklist's four dimensions are correctness, security, maintainability, human understanding. The trap keeps delivery metrics, which measure a change's cost, not whether it is safe to ship.

items.sourceSection: Glossary

points.v: Captured set of known symptom-to-cause-to-action paths letting a team resolve recurring operational issues without the Architect
Named definition of who handles what and when an operational issue leaves the team

quiz.q: The same three recurring failures pull the Architect back in every week, and when something larger appears nobody knows at what point it should stop being the team's problem.
options: A runbook of symptom-to-cause-to-action paths, plus a named escalation path defining who handles what and when.
A weekly office-hours slot with the Architect, plus a postmortem after each recurring failure.
A runbook alone - once symptoms and actions are captured, who to escalate to follows from severity.
An on-call rotation covering the team, plus a permission posture that blocks the actions causing those failures.
quiz.why: Two artifacts: a runbook resolves recurring issues without the Architect; an escalation path names who handles what and when. The runbook-alone trap leaves that handoff undefined.

items.sourceSection: Glossary

points.v: A single team baseline (e.g. project CLAUDE.md, agreed tools, permission posture) that every member starts from, instead of individual setups that drift apart

quiz.q: Every developer has their own project file, tool set and permission prompts; sessions behave differently per machine and nobody can reproduce a teammate's result.
options: Standardize the model default only; project files, tooling and permission prompts are legitimately personal preference.
Package each developer's configuration as a plugin, so the differences at least become versioned and auditable.
Require a weekly configuration reset, so drift is bounded to seven days before everyone returns to defaults.
Define one baseline every member starts from: the project CLAUDE.md, agreed tools, and a shared permission posture.
quiz.why: A team environment is a single shared baseline. The versioned-per-developer trap preserves the drift it claims to fix - auditable divergence is still divergence.

items.sourceSection: Improving developer workflows with AI tooling
items.lead: Human understanding is the fourth verification dimension

points.v: The author must be able to explain what shipped
Failure to watch for: engineers accepting AI output they no longer fully understand because it looks right and passes a check
Correctness, security, and maintainability alone do not satisfy the verification checklist

items.logic: Output that is correct, secure, maintainable, and passes the regression and eval suites looks fully verified — but passing checks is exactly the condition under which the subtle failure hides.

quiz.q: A change is correct, secure and maintainable and passes the regression and eval suites; its author would need to re-derive one function to answer questions about it in review.
options: Ship it - passing the regression and eval suites is stronger evidence than any individual author's recall.
Not yet verified - the author must be able to explain what shipped before it goes out.
Ship it - correct, secure and maintainable is the full bar, and the green checks confirm all three.
Hold it until that function is documented; the gap is documentation, not anything the verification checklist covers.
quiz.why: Human understanding is the fourth verification dimension. The three-dimensions-plus-green-checks trap describes exactly the condition under which an accepted but unexplained change hides.

items.sourceSection: Sources
items.lead: Org plugin management spans these mechanics

points.v: Plugin marketplaces
Group assignment
Install preferences (required / default install)
Hide and deprecate behavior
Manual upload
GitHub sync
Update
Removal

quiz.q: An admin says the only way to get a shared toolset to a subset of teams is to hand out a zip for people to install, and that retiring an old one means deleting it for everyone.
options: Correct - upload and removal are the org-level controls; targeting and retirement are handled by each team locally.
Half right - assignment by group exists, but retirement still requires removal; hiding and deprecating are not available.
Wrong twice - group assignment, install preferences, GitHub sync, and hide-and-deprecate behavior all exist alongside manual upload and removal.
Wrong - sync from a connected GitHub repository is the only supported source, so manual upload is not offered.
quiz.why: Org plugin management spans marketplaces, group assignment, install preferences, hide/deprecate, manual upload, GitHub sync, update and removal. The upload-only trap ignores both targeting and retirement.
